courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
question: Why does the sort key put the tile ID in the high bits and the depth in the low bits, rather than the reverse?
options: So a single sort groups instances by tile first, and orders each tile's instances by depth
Because depth needs more than 32 bits of precision
So that far Gaussians are drawn first, as in the painter's algorithm
Because radix sort only looks at the low 32 bits
explain: Sorting by a combined key orders by its high bits first. With tile ID on top, all instances of a tile become contiguous, and ties within a tile are broken by depth, giving a front-to-back list per tile from one global sort.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Finding room for the tag: wide CAS, spare bits, indices
question: Your nodes come from a pool of at most 4 billion entries. Which layout lets you avoid both double-width CAS and spare pointer bits?
options: 32-bit array index and 32-bit tag in one 64-bit word
64-bit pointer and 64-bit tag
48-bit pointer and 16-bit tag
explain: This is the array-index option from Michael and Scott: an index into a node array needs only 32 bits for up to 2^32 nodes, leaving 32 bits for the counter, and an ordinary 64-bit CAS covers both.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
question: A colleague's ablation script sorts each run's per-query scores from best to worst before running a paired t-test. The test reports p < 0.001 for a stage. What went wrong?
options: Sorting broke the pairing: deltas now compare different queries, so the p-value is meaningless
Nothing; a paired t-test is invariant to the order of the queries
The t-test should have been replaced by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The p-value is fine but should be divided by the number of queries
explain: Pairing works only if position i holds the same query in both runs. Sorting each run separately pairs the best query of one run with the best of the other, removing query-level noise artificially. Align runs by query id before differencing.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench Verified, Lite, and tests that reject correct fixes
question: SWE-bench Lite's filters remove multi-file patches, short issues and tests that check error messages. What is the main effect on what the score measures?
options: Lite removes tasks whose tests are wrong, so its scores are more valid
Lite makes tasks easier and more self-contained, so its scores are not comparable to full SWE-bench scores
Lite adds contamination protection
Lite has the same difficulty mix but costs less
explain: Lite was built for cheaper iteration. Its filters select self-contained, simpler bug fixes, and OpenAI found within-difficulty performance barely changed, so Lite's higher scores mostly reflect an easier task mix.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Tool calls on the wire: tool_use, tool_result and stop_reason
question: An OpenAI-style function_call arrives with arguments '{"city": "Oslo"'. What should a robust harness do?
options: Pass the string to the tool and let it fail
Try to parse the JSON; on failure, return an error result with the same call_id explaining the parse error
Silently drop the call and call the model again
Abort the whole run
explain: Arguments arrive as a JSON string that can be malformed. Parse and validate before execution, and on failure answer the call with an error result so the model can correct itself. Dropping the call leaves it unanswered; aborting wastes a recoverable run. Strict schema modes reduce, but harness validation still guards the boundary.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
question: A coding assistant learns three things in one session: the user ran the test suite at 14:02 and it failed; the repo uses pnpm, not npm; the user prefers short answers. Which are best stored as semantic memories?
options: All three, because everything the user says is a fact about the user
Only the test failure, because it is the most recent event
The pnpm fact and the short-answer preference; the test run is an episodic event
None; semantic memory only holds facts about the outside world
explain: The pnpm choice and the answer-length preference stay true until changed, so they are semantic facts. The failing test run at 14:02 is an event tied to a time: episodic. It may matter later ("what failed yesterday?") but it is not a standing fact. CoALA's semantic memory covers knowledge about the agent and the user too, not only the outside world.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
question: A user's running sum of importance since the last reflection is 50. Each new event in a quiet week is rated 2. Using the paper's threshold, roughly how many such events until the next reflection fires?
options: About 50 events, since the sum must exceed 150
About 3 events, since reflection fires two or three times a day
Never, because low-importance events are not counted
About 75 events, since the threshold is 150 and each event adds 2
explain: The sum must climb from 50 to over 150, so it needs more than 100 more points: 51 events at 2 each take it to 152. Two or three reflections a day was what the paper observed in its busy simulated town, not a fixed schedule. 75 events ignores the 50 already accumulated. Every event's importance is summed.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling
question: Candidates are correct half the time (p = 0.5). A verifier has TPR 0.8 and FPR 0.2. What fraction of shipped answers are correct if the agent abstains whenever nothing passes?
explain: Shipped answers are all passers, so accuracy is precision: 0.5(0.8) / (0.5(0.8) + 0.5(0.2)) = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
question: Why did SWE-RL's continuous similarity reward beat a binary exact-match reward?
options: The binary reward allowed the model to hack the tests
Exact match is too slow to compute at RL scale
Exact matches with the developer patch were so rare that the binary reward stayed near zero and gave almost no signal
GRPO cannot normalize binary rewards
explain: Real patches vary, so an exact match almost never happens; the discrete reward averaged about zero. The similarity score gives credit for being close, which the paper says captures partial correctness and incremental improvements.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
question: A GNoME-style loop is in round 3. To save compute, a teammate proposes retraining only on candidates that DFT confirmed as stable. What is the main problem?
options: The model would never see its false positives, so it cannot learn to stop recommending them
Stable structures have no energy label
DFT results cannot be used as training data
It would make the hull computation slower
explain: The filter's job is to separate stable from unstable near the decision boundary. The DFT-confirmed failures are exactly the examples where it was wrong; throwing them away removes the signal that raises precision round after round.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
question: A SynthID-style tournament is run with 3 candidates per match instead of 2, to strengthen the watermark. What changes?
options: Nothing: any tournament preserves the model's distribution
The watermark gets weaker because ties are more common
Detection now requires running the language model
The watermark gets stronger but the output distribution is no longer exactly the model's, so quality can drop
explain: The paper proves two competitors per match is single-token non-distortionary and that more competitors make tournament sampling distortionary, with a stronger watermark. That is SynthID's distortionary configuration. Detection still only needs the key and the g-functions.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: From trace to replayable workload: slots, syncs and varints
question: In the example, why does T1's second malloc (into slot 1) need SYNC_R 3 even though T1 never talks to T2 in the program's code?
options: Because slot 1 was last freed by T2, and without the wait T1 could refill slot 1 before T2 frees it in replay
Because every malloc after a thread switch needs a sync
Because syncs keep the threads' CPU usage balanced
Because the master thread must always run last
explain: In replay, slot 1 still holds T1's first block until T2's FREE 1 runs. If T1 refilled the slot first, T2 would free the new block. trace2wl adds a sync when a slot's owner changes (and when a new thread first appears); T1's FREE 2 needed none.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
question: Why is reach-dist(p, o) defined as max(k-distance(o), d(p, o)) instead of just d(p, o)?
options: To make LOF symmetric, so LOF(p, o) = LOF(o, p)
To smooth out statistical fluctuations: points very close to o all get the same distance, so tiny gaps inside clusters do not create huge densities
To make LOF equal to the k-nearest-neighbor distance
To guarantee LOF is always at least 1
explain: Breunig et al. introduce the reachability distance so that for points near o the actual distance is replaced by o's k-distance, which reduces fluctuations in d(p, o). The parameter k controls how strong this smoothing is.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
question: Redo reaches LSN 60 (T2's update of P1). The DPT says P1 recLSN 10, and P1 read from disk has pageLSN 60. What happens?
options: Redo it, because 60 is at least recLSN 10
Skip it, because T2 is a loser
Skip it, because the page's pageLSN shows the change is already on disk
Undo it immediately, because the page holds uncommitted data
explain: Passing the recLSN test only means the change might be missing. Reading the page settles it: pageLSN 60 means this update is already there. Loser status plays no role in redo, and undo waits for the undo pass.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
question: In the toy, which configuration does a codebase have if one embed() helper hard-codes the query input type and is used both to build the index and to search it?
options: Everything in query mode
No roles
Everything in document mode
Correct roles
explain: Both sides go through query mode, so the stored documents are encoded as if they were queries. In the toy that ranks the duplicate questions first (0.99) and drops the answers to 0.82.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
question: An API allows 60 requests per minute using a token bucket with a small capacity. At 12:00:00 you send 60 requests at once. What is the most likely outcome?
options: All 60 succeed because the minute has just started
About half succeed because limits are checked every 30 seconds
A few succeed (up to the bucket capacity) and the rest get 429, even though you sent only 60 in that minute
None succeed because bursts are always rejected
explain: A token bucket does not reset at the top of the minute. It holds at most b tokens and refills at 1 per second here. A burst larger than b is rejected beyond the capacity. Anthropic explicitly notes that 60 RPM may be enforced as 1 request per second.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
question: After a crash, your batch script restarts and immediately submits a new batch for all items. What risk did it create, and what prevents it?
options: None; the provider deduplicates batches automatically
Results of the old batch will overwrite the new one
If the first batch was already submitted, every item is processed and billed twice; persist the batch id right after creation and resume polling it on restart
The new batch will be rejected because custom_ids must be globally unique
explain: Nothing in the docs says batches are deduplicated across submissions; custom_id only needs to be unique within a batch. Saving the batch id before polling makes the submission step idempotent: on restart, look up the stored id and resume.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
question: Why does Tokio use per-worker local queues plus stealing instead of a single shared run queue?
options: A shared queue cannot hold more than 256 tasks
Most pushes and pops then touch only the worker's own queue, avoiding contention on one shared structure, while stealing still balances load
Stealing guarantees strict FIFO order across the whole runtime
Local queues let the OS preempt long-running tasks
explain: A single queue is simple but every worker contends on it. Sharding into local queues removes most contention; work stealing (and the global queue for overflow and outside wakeups) keeps idle workers busy. Ordering becomes looser, which Tokio's docs say explicitly.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses
question: Eight threads spin waiting for a lock flag to become 0, each running `while lock.compare_exchange(0, 1, ...).is_err() {}`. The lock is held for a long time. What is the main performance problem?
options: Each failing CAS still takes exclusive ownership of the flag's cache line, so the waiters keep stealing it from each other and from the holder
compare_exchange cannot fail, so the loop never ends
The CAS writes 1 even when it fails, so it corrupts the lock
Nothing; failed CAS attempts are as cheap as loads
explain: A failed CAS does not change the value, but it still demands exclusive access to the line, so eight spinners bounce it between cores and slow down the holder too. The usual fix is to spin on a plain load until the flag reads 0 and only then try the CAS (test and test-and-set).

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Scoring a tagger: average precision and mAP
question: You raise the decision threshold for Dog from 0.5 to 0.8 without changing the model. What happens to Dog AP?
options: It is unchanged, because AP depends only on the ranking of scores
It rises, because fewer false positives are output
It falls, because fewer positives are detected
It becomes undefined
explain: AP is computed from the order of clips by score, sweeping every possible cut-off. A threshold only matters when you convert scores into hard tags for a product, which is a separate decision.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tokens, budgets and when to stop
question: An agent's per-run cost grows much faster than linearly as you raise its step cap from 10 to 40. Which change most directly addresses the cause?
options: Use a model with a larger context window
Raise the sampling temperature so it finds answers sooner
Split the work across subagents with separate contexts and return short summaries
Ask the model to write shorter search queries
explain: Each call re-reads the whole context, so input tokens grow roughly with the square of the step count. Shorter contexts (subagents returning summaries) cut the quadratic term. A larger window allows more growth rather than less; query length is a tiny share of r.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding
question: Decode on a laptop is memory-bandwidth-bound. Which change gives the biggest speedup ceiling for the same model?
options: Doubling the number of CPU cores used for the matmuls
Storing weights in 2 bits instead of 16
Switching attention to a faster softmax implementation
Using FP32 accumulators instead of FP16
explain: When decode is bandwidth-bound, time per token is about bytes read divided by bandwidth. Going from 16 to 2 bits reads 8x fewer weight bytes. More cores help only when compute is the bottleneck, and softmax or accumulator changes do not reduce weight traffic.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
question: After packing 2B4T's linear weights into 2 bits, which part of the model is now the largest single block of weights?
options: The attention Q and K projections
The FFN weights, still 2.08 GB
The BF16 embedding and tied output head, about 0.66 GB
The RMSNorm parameters
explain: The 128,256 x 2560 embedding is 328M parameters at 2 bytes: 0.66 GB, versus 0.52 GB for all 2.08B ternary weights. Because the embeddings are tied, the output head reads that matrix every token, which is why large vocabularies matter more once the rest is ternary.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
question: You replace a well-predicted branch (99.9 percent accuracy) that skips an expensive computation with a branchless select that always does the computation. Most likely result?
options: Faster, branches are always slow
Same speed, the select is free
Slower, because the expensive side now runs every time
Undefined behavior
explain: A well-predicted branch costs almost nothing, and it lets the CPU skip the expensive side entirely. Agner Fog: a conditional jump is preferred when it lets you avoid a lengthy calculation of the side that is not chosen.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
question: A compaction merges L1 into L2 and finds a tombstone for key 42. L3 has a file covering keys 30 to 60. What must the compaction do with the tombstone?
options: Drop it, since the newer data has already been merged
Keep it in the output, because an older version of 42 may still exist in L3
Delete the L3 file covering key 42
Convert it into a regular value with an empty string
explain: L3 is older data. If the tombstone were dropped, a later Get(42) would miss in L1 and L2, reach L3 and return the old, deleted value. The marker must travel down until no lower level can hold the key.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
question: In the simulation, LRU loses more hot hits during the scan than clock-sweep with a cap of 5. What is the main reason?
options: Hot pages build up usage counts, so the hand must pass them several times before evicting them, while scan pages are evictable after one pass
Clock-sweep evicts scan pages first because it knows they are sequential
Clock-sweep has more frames than LRU in the simulation
LRU evicts dirty pages first
explain: Both policies have 100 frames and neither knows about scans. The difference is the counter: a page hit repeatedly survives several sweeps, while a page loaded once with count 1 is evictable after one sweep. It is still not perfect, which is why its bar does not reach 100%.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
question: Why can a byte-level model never hit an out-of-vocabulary input?
options: Its vocabulary is the 256 possible byte values, and any UTF-8 text is a sequence of bytes
It learns new tokens during inference
It maps rare characters to an UNK id
UTF-8 has only 256 characters
explain: Every string, in any script, is a sequence of bytes 0 to 255, so the input vocabulary is complete by construction. UTF-8 covers all of Unicode by using 1 to 4 bytes per character, not by having 256 characters.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
question: A product mainly processes noisy user text (typos, odd casing) in many languages, and needs character-level edits. Which statement best matches the evidence in this course?
options: A BPE model with more training data will close the gap on character tasks
Byte-level models with patching are a strong fit; they were more robust to noise and far better at character manipulation
Byte models only help for English
Byte models are always faster at inference than BPE models
explain: BLT beat a same-data BPE model by 7.4 points on noised HellaSwag and by 26.6 on CUTE, while Llama 3.1, trained on far more data, scored lower on CUTE. Speed depends on patch size and implementation; the authors note wall-clock parity is not yet shown.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
question: Your unsafe-backed parser passes `cargo miri test` with no errors. What can you conclude?
options: The parser can never cause undefined behavior
The inputs your tests ran did not trigger any UB that Miri detects
The parser is safe to mark `Sync`
The borrow checker has verified the unsafe blocks
explain: Miri checks the executions it actually performs. Untested inputs, and kinds of unsoundness Miri does not model, can still hide bugs. It raises confidence; it does not prove soundness.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
question: An L1 has a 4-cycle hit time and a 10% miss rate, and every miss costs 100 more cycles. What is the AMAT?
options: 4.4 cycles
10.4 cycles
14 cycles
40 cycles
explain: AMAT = 4 + 0.10 x 100 = 14 cycles. 4.4 forgets that the penalty is 100 cycles, not 4; 40 multiplies instead of adding. Note how a 10% miss rate more than triples the hit time.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
question: Which statement about error nodes in an attribution graph is correct?
options: They receive edges from the features that caused the error
They have outgoing edges but no incoming edges, and are not interpretable
They are removed before pruning because they carry no information
They only appear at the final layer
explain: An error node holds the gap between the true MLP output and the CLT output at one position and layer. It feeds later nodes, but the method has no way to attribute into it, so it appears from nowhere. There is one per position and layer, and pruning keeps them.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
question: Graph A has completeness 0.80 and replacement 0.61; graph B has 0.78 and 0.37. What does B's lower replacement score mean?
options: Fewer of B's full paths from embeddings to the logit avoid error nodes
B's features are less interpretable
B used a higher pruning threshold
B's logits are wrong
explain: Both have most node inputs explained (completeness), but replacement only credits complete embedding-to-logit paths that never pass through an error node. Longer per-layer paths have more chances to hit one.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
question: You only have logs from one fixed production ranker that never changes the order for a given query. Which method can still estimate position bias from these logs alone?
options: Intervention harvesting
Regression EM, using features shared by documents at different ranks
Identifier-based EM over (query, document) pairs
None: a swap experiment is mandatory
explain: Harvesting needs several rankers, and identifier-based EM needs each pair at multiple ranks. Regression EM only needs similar feature vectors to appear at different ranks, which happens across queries even with one deterministic ranker, though it relies on the regression model being right.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: SigLIP's sigmoid loss and how CLIP training scales
question: In the SigLIP toy at t = 50 and b = -12, the cat photo and the dog caption have cosine 0.26, giving a logit of +1.0. What would lowering the bias b from -12 to -14 do to that cell?
options: Nothing, because the bias cancels in the sigmoid
It raises its match probability, increasing the loss
It changes only the positive cells
It lowers its logit to -1.0, so the pair is now judged a non-match and its loss falls
explain: The logit is t times cosine plus b: 50 x 0.26 - 14 = -1.0, so sigma gives 0.27 match probability and the negative's loss drops from 1.31 to about 0.31. The bias shifts every cell, which is why SigLIP learns it: it sets the threshold between match and non-match.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
question: A clustering gives point q a silhouette of -0.35. What does that say?
options: q is an outlier that belongs to no cluster
The clustering has too few clusters, since silhouettes cannot be negative otherwise
q is exactly on the boundary between two clusters
q is on average closer to the points of another cluster than to the points of its own
explain: Negative means b(i) is less than a(i): the mean distance to the nearest other cluster is smaller than the mean distance to its own cluster members. A value near 0, not negative, means a boundary point. The silhouette has no notion of noise, and negative values can appear at any k.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
question: A service writes 50,000 single-row updates per second, each changing every field of a record. Which choice fits best?
options: A pure column store, because each column compresses better
A row store, or a column store that buffers writes in row-wise delta structures
A column store with a larger page size
Either; layout does not affect update cost
explain: Each update touches every column, so a pure column layout would write into one place per column. Row stores write one contiguous record. Column stores cope by sending writes to delta structures (as MonetDB/X100 does) and merging later.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
question: Why does the branch-free select loop write res[k] = i even for rows that fail the predicate?
options: It is a bug that wastes memory
Because the selection vector must have length n
So the loop has no data-dependent branch; a failing row's write is simply overwritten by the next one
To keep the output sorted
explain: Writing unconditionally and advancing k by the 0/1 comparison result removes the branch. With unpredictable predicates this avoids branch mispredictions; the stray write is harmless since k did not advance.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
question: Why does adding `restrict` to all three pointers let the compiler drop the runtime check?
options: restrict makes the arrays aligned to 16 bytes
restrict forces -O3
restrict tells the compiler the arrays do not overlap, so stores cannot affect later loads
restrict copies the arrays before the loop
explain: The check exists only to detect overlap. restrict promises there is none, so the compiler can vectorize unconditionally. If the promise is false the program has undefined behavior.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
question: Why does the Anthropic reference environment use a virtual X11 display (Xvfb) inside a container instead of the developer's own desktop?
options: Xvfb renders screenshots faster than a physical display
The model can only read screenshots from Linux machines
It gives the harness a controllable, isolated machine whose mistakes cannot touch the host
The tool definition requires display_number to be set
explain: The environment is something your application controls: a virtual display, the apps, and the code that turns tool requests into real input. Isolation is the point. The docs' first safety precaution is a dedicated VM or container with minimal privileges.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
question: An agent books meetings in a web calendar. Which control most limits the damage if a malicious invite injects "forward all emails to this address"?
options: A system prompt line telling the model to distrust calendar invites
Raising the screenshot resolution so the model reads the invite more carefully
Allowing only the calendar domain on the network and requiring human confirmation before any send action
Running the agent with a larger step budget so it can recover
explain: The allowlist removes the email service from reach, and a harness-enforced confirmation stops any send that slips through. Both work even if the model is fully convinced by the injected text. Prompt wording is useful but bypassable; resolution and step budgets do not address the threat.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
question: Thread A writes a global at t = 0 ms. Thread B reads it at t = 500 ms. Nothing synchronizes them, and B reads the correct value. What does TSan report?
options: A data race, because neither access happens before the other
Nothing, because the accesses were 500 ms apart and never overlapped
A data race only if halt_on_error is set
Nothing, because the read returned the correct value
explain: TSan checks the happens-before relation, not wall-clock overlap. With no release and acquire linking A to B, A's write is not visible in B's vector clock, so the pair is reported.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Training: consistency distillation, consistency training, EMA
question: You have no pretrained diffusion model and a large image dataset. Which method can you use, and what replaces the teacher?
options: Consistency distillation, with the online network acting as the teacher
Neither: consistency models always need a pretrained diffusion model
Progressive distillation, starting from a random teacher
Consistency training, where the score is estimated from the known clean image as -(x_t - x)/t^2, giving the pair x + t_n+1 z and x + t_n z
explain: CT needs only data. Using the clean image that generated the noisy point gives an unbiased score estimate, and one Euler step with it lands on x + t_n z with the same noise draw. CD and progressive distillation both need a trained teacher.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
question: Two users concurrently edit a shared document's title and description; neither saw the other's change. Under causal consistency, what is guaranteed about the order other readers see these edits in?
options: Readers may see them in different orders, since they are concurrent
Every reader sees them in the same order
The edit that was invoked first in real time is seen first
Each reader sees them in the order they reached the leader
explain: No causal path links the two edits, so causal consistency lets replicas apply them in either order. A single agreed order is what sequential consistency adds; real-time ordering is what linearizability adds. Convergent variants only require agreement eventually.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
question: Which property does a consistent hash give that hash mod N does not?
options: Keys are spread evenly when the server set is fixed
Adding a server moves keys only onto the new server, never between existing servers
Every key is stored on more than one server
Lookups need no hash function at all
explain: Both schemes spread keys evenly for a fixed set of servers. What consistent hashing adds is monotonicity: when a server is added, the only keys that move are those that now belong to it. Replication is a separate choice layered on top.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
question: An engineer writes `bool: { filter: [work_auth US], should: [skills go, skills rust] }` meaning "authorized AND (Go OR Rust)". What does the query actually return?
options: Authorized candidates who know Go or Rust
Authorized candidates, with Go and Rust only raising the score; candidates with neither are still returned
Nothing, because should requires all clauses to match
Candidates who know Go or Rust, whether authorized or not
explain: Because a filter clause is present, minimum_should_match defaults to 0 and the should clauses are optional. Fix it with "minimum_should_match": 1, or move a nested bool with the two should clauses into the filter list.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
question: Why does MRV pick the variable with the fewest remaining values first?
options: That variable is the most likely to cause a failure, so the search finds dead branches near the top of the tree
It makes each node cheaper to expand because there are fewer values to loop over
It guarantees the first solution found is optimal
It keeps more values available for the other variables
explain: MRV is fail-first. Every variable must be assigned anyway, so tackling the most constrained one early exposes dead branches high up, where pruning removes the largest subtrees. Option D describes LCV, the value-ordering rule, which aims at success instead.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
question: You run the same CP-SAT model twice on an 8-core laptop with default parameters and get two different optimal schedules with the same objective. What is the most likely reason?
options: A bug: optimal solutions must be unique
The second run hit a time limit
Presolve removed constraints differently on the second run, making one schedule invalid
The default uses all cores, and parallel workers race, so which optimum is reported can vary between runs
explain: Several schedules can share the optimal objective. With num_workers at its default of 0, CP-SAT uses all cores, and whichever worker finds a solution first in a given run can differ. Both answers are correct; set num_workers = 1 (and a fixed seed) when you need repeatable output.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement
question: A pod has one container with requests of cpu 200m and memory 256Mi, and limits of cpu 1 and memory 256Mi. What is its QoS class?
options: Guaranteed, because the memory request equals the memory limit
BestEffort, because the CPU is not pinned
Burstable, because the CPU request and limit differ
Guaranteed, because both requests are set
explain: Guaranteed requires request to equal limit for both CPU and memory, in every container. Memory matches here but CPU does not (200m against 1000m), so the pod is Burstable: evicted after BestEffort pods and before Guaranteed ones, and only while it is using more than its requests.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
question: Location is a multi-valued list currently holding [US]. The user says *also Canada*. What should the new value be?
options: [Canada]
null
dontcare
[US, Canada]
explain: With a multi-valued slot, *also* adds to the list. [Canada] would be the result of *Canada instead*. The schema has to declare the slot multi-valued for this to work at all.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
question: On a task, early-answering AOC is 0.02. What is the most accurate reading?
options: The CoT is 98% faithful
The model's answer is nearly always the same with or without the rest of its CoT, so the reasoning is mostly post-hoc
The model makes mistakes in 2% of its CoTs
Truncating the CoT almost always changes the answer
explain: AOC near 0 means the match curve sits near 100% from the start: the answer was set before the reasoning was read. That is evidence of post-hoc reasoning, not a faithfulness percentage. Option D describes a high AOC.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
question: Someone optimizes the kernel from 24 ms to 12 ms. What is the new batch time and the new SM utilization?
options: 49 ms, utilization 24.5 percent
30.5 ms, utilization unchanged at 39.3 percent
49 ms, utilization 39.3 percent
37 ms, utilization 32.4 percent
explain: 20 + 16 + 12 + 1 = 49 ms, and the SMs are now busy 12 of those 49 ms, which is 24.5 percent. Halving the kernel bought 19.7 percent of wall time and made the imbalance worse. The 37 ms of host and copy time is where the remaining win lives.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
question: You chunk the host decode too, and measure the host stage at 8.00 ms per chunk (kernel stays 6.00 ms). What paces the pipeline and what is the 4-chunk time?
options: The host, at 8.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms
The kernel, at 6.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 6.00 = 36.25 ms
Neither; the host runs on a different device so it does not enter the makespan
The H2D copy, since it is the stage directly after the host
explain: The host is just another single-server stage in the pipeline, and the makespan is set by whichever stage is largest. At 8.00 ms it overtakes the 6.00 ms kernel, giving (8.00 + 4.00 + 6.00 + 0.25) + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms, with 2.00 ms of SM idle per chunk. The fix is more host parallelism (more decode threads or loader workers), not more CUDA streams.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: A query is 20 tokens and a passage is 600 tokens. Using a BERT tokenizer with max_length 512 and truncation=True, how many passage tokens remain?
explain: Three special tokens ([CLS] and two [SEP]) plus 20 query tokens use 23 positions, leaving 512 - 23 = 489 for the passage. longest_first trims the longer side, which is the passage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: Why does Margin-MSE train on the score difference instead of asking the student to reproduce the teacher's raw score?
options: Because the teacher's raw scores are not available after training
Because MSE cannot be computed on raw scores
Because the margin is always positive
Because different architectures produce scores on very different ranges, and ranking only depends on order and gaps
explain: The paper observed that cross-encoders, dot-product models and others have distinct score ranges. Matching margins lets the student keep its natural range while learning the teacher's preferences. The margin can even be negative when the teacher disagrees with the label.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: A TiledMMA uses the SM80 16x8x16 FP32-accumulate atom with a 2x2 layout of atoms (4 warps) and no value repetition. How many FP32 accumulators does each thread hold?
explain: Each atom is one warp computing 16x8 = 128 accumulators over 32 threads, so 4 per thread. A 2x2 layout of atoms adds more warps, not more values per thread: 128 threads cover 32x16 = 512 accumulators, still 4 each.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: A vendor ships a card with a CXL controller and 256 GB of DRAM and no compute engine. Which protocols must it implement?
options: CXL.cache only
CXL.io and CXL.mem
CXL.io and CXL.cache
CXL.mem only, because CXL.io is optional
explain: This is a Type 3 memory expander. It needs CXL.io for discovery and configuration (every device does) and CXL.mem so the host can load and store its memory. It has no cache of host memory, so CXL.cache is not needed.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: Pond allocates a VM's predicted untouched memory from the pool and exposes it as a zero-core NUMA node. Why the zero-core node rather than mixing pool and local memory in one node?
options: Because CXL memory cannot be part of a node that has CPUs
Because the guest OS then prefers its local node and touches the pool only when it needs more, so correctly predicted untouched memory costs nothing
Because hypervisors cannot map CXL memory into guest page tables
Because it makes the pool memory persistent
explain: With a uniform address space the guest would scatter allocations across pool and local memory. A CPU-less node is a fallback in Linux's default policy, so the guest fills local memory first; if the untouched-memory prediction is right, the pool slices are never touched.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: You start DoReMi from uniform reference weights on a corpus where one domain is tiny. After one round, results are no better than baseline. What is the paper's recommended next move?
options: Run iterated DoReMi: train a new reference model on the round-1 weights and run again
Increase the proxy to 1B parameters
Set the smoothing c to 0 so weak domains disappear
Copy the published Pile weights
explain: On GLaM, round 1 from uniform weights was only comparable to the baseline, and round 2 matched downstream-tuned weights. A suboptimal reference gives a suboptimal excess loss; iterating fixes the reference. Bigger proxies did worse in the paper.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: In `soa<8> Point pts[...]` (float x, y, z), what is the byte offset of `pts[17].z` from the start of the array?
explain: Block 17 // 8 = 2, lane 17 % 8 = 1. Each block is 96 bytes and z is the third 32-byte run. Offset = 2 x 96 + 2 x 32 + 1 x 4 = 260. 212 is the AoS answer (17 x 12 + 8), 204 is where record 17 starts in AoS, and 68 is plain SoA (17 x 4).

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Where a GPU inference stack loses bitwise equality
question: A team sets torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True and finds that two runs of the same model on the same machine give different outputs. What is happening?
options: cuDNN silently drops to a lower precision while benchmarking.
Benchmarking reseeds the RNG, so the weights initialize differently.
Timing noise can make the benchmark pick a different algorithm on a later run, and different algorithms accumulate in different orders.
The GPU clock frequency changes the hardware rounding mode.
explain: The benchmark times candidate algorithms and keeps the winner per shape. Noise in that timing can crown a different winner on another run, and two algorithms with different reduction trees give different bits. Setting benchmark = False pins the choice, but the pinned algorithm may itself be nondeterministic unless the deterministic flags are set too.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
question: Jepsen-style fault injection and DST both inject partitions and crashes into real code. What does DST add that changes day-to-day debugging most?
options: It tests a formal model instead of the code, so it is exhaustive
Any failing run can be replayed exactly from its seed
It needs no changes to how the system does I/O
It runs on real hardware, so timing is realistic
explain: Determinism is the key addition: a failure becomes a seed you can replay, step through and add logging to. DST does test the real code (not a model), it usually *does* require routing I/O through simulated interfaces, and its timing is simulated, not real.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
question: Which system is the *weakest* fit for designing DST in from the start?
options: A new replicated log written in-house with its own network and disk layer
A large existing service built on many third-party clients, thread pools and direct system calls
A consensus library whose I/O already goes through small traits
A storage engine with a single-threaded event loop
explain: Designing DST in requires every source of nondeterminism to be pluggable, which is hard to retrofit across many dependencies and threads. The Antithesis docs call it generally impractical for systems already in production; that is the case a deterministic hypervisor targets. The other three are close to the FoundationDB and TigerBeetle shape.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism
question: A disaggregated deployment meets TTFT easily but misses TPOT at high load, and decode GPUs are near their KV memory limit. What is the most sensible next change?
options: Add prefill instances
Add decode capacity (more decode instances or more parallelism per decode instance)
Merge the pools back into a colocated deployment
Increase the prefill batch size
explain: TPOT is decided by the decode side. Decode batch size is bounded by KV memory, and DistServe notes that scaling the decoding instance with model parallelism (or memory techniques like PagedAttention and GQA) lets it batch more. Extra prefill instances would just send more KV caches to an already full decode pool.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
question: HNSW passes only the final L search results to its pruning step, while Vamana passes every node visited during the search. What does that change?
options: Vamana's graph has no reverse edges
Nothing, the two sets are identical
Vamana sees far-away nodes from early in the path as candidates, so it can create long-range edges without a hierarchy
HNSW becomes slower to build
explain: Nodes visited early in a greedy walk are far from p. Giving RobustPrune those candidates (together with alpha > 1) lets p keep some long jumps. HNSW gets long jumps from its upper layers instead, which DiskANN avoids because each layer would mean more disk reads.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
question: A recommendation service sends one query at a time to a GPU CAGRA index, and the GPU is mostly idle. Which setting addresses this?
options: Multi-CTA search, which spreads one query across several thread blocks
A larger team_size
A smaller graph_degree
Single-CTA with a persistent kernel
explain: Single-CTA maps a query to one block, so a batch of 1 uses a sliver of the GPU. Multi-CTA assigns several CTAs to one query, each expanding a parent, which the paper designed for batch sizes of about 1 to 100. cuVS AUTO selects it for small batches.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Why does KTO estimate $z_0$ from mismatched (prompt, other example's output) pairs instead of each example's own output?
options: Because own outputs are usually chosen to be clearly good or bad, so their rewards are unrepresentatively large
Because mismatched pairs need no forward pass
Because the own output's log-ratio is always zero
Because it makes the estimate unbiased
explain: The paper says matched outputs have often been deliberately picked as canonically good or bad, giving high-magnitude rewards that would skew the reference point. The mismatched estimate still costs an extra forward pass and is explicitly biased (clamping adds upward bias), but it is cheap and stable.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
question: A backfill uses insert-if-absent. A user deletes subscription S: the dual write deletes it from both stores. A backfill worker had read S from the old store just before the delete, and writes it to the new store just after. What happens?
options: S comes back to life in the new store, because after the delete there is no row to block the insert
Nothing: insert-if-absent skips S because it already exists
The insert fails with a foreign-key error
The old store also gets S back
explain: Insert-if-absent treats a missing row as never copied, but here it is missing because it was deleted. The fix is to remember deletes (a tombstone row or a version that marks deletion), or to order the copy against the change log so the delete is applied after the copied row.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
question: You are writing a script that teammates will run for years across kernel upgrades. It counts file opens per process. Which probe should you choose first?
options: kprobe:do_sys_openat2, because kprobes can reach any function
uprobe on libc's open wrapper
tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat, because tracepoints are stable interfaces in the kernel source
profile:hz:99, because sampling has the lowest overhead
explain: Tracepoints are placed by kernel developers and meant to keep a stable interface. Internal function names that kprobes target can be renamed or change arguments between versions. A libc uprobe misses programs that make the syscall directly, and sampling would miss most opens.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: A bpftrace script printing one line per network packet starts reporting lost events under load. What is the best fix?
options: Replace printf with a map aggregation such as @[comm] = count() or hist(), so per-event data stays in the kernel
Increase max_strlen
Switch the probe from tracepoint to kprobe
Run two copies of the script
explain: Lost events mean user space cannot drain the ring buffer fast enough. Raising perf_rb_pages only buys headroom; aggregating in a map removes the per-event traffic entirely.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training
question: A post-training int8 model loses 30 points of accuracy. Inspecting one conv layer, you find output channel ranges from 0.003 to 4.0, and the converter used one scale per tensor. What is the cheapest fix to try first?
options: Switch to quantization-aware training
Increase the calibration set from 200 to 20,000 images
Quantize activations per channel
Use per-channel weight scales
explain: A 1,300x range spread across channels is the classic per-tensor failure. Per-channel weight scales fix it with no training, and the whitepaper shows they recover MobileNetV2 to within about 2 points. More calibration data affects activation ranges, not weight ranges. QAT works too but costs a training run.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
question: Compute: a test set has two problems. Response 1 is 400 tokens, first correct at 100. Response 2 is 800 tokens, first correct at 800. What is the outcome efficiency?
explain: $(100/400 + 800/800)/2 = (0.25 + 1.0)/2 = 0.625$. Response 2 needed all its tokens, so it counts as fully efficient even though it is long.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: The supply voltage rises from 230 V to 240 V while every appliance stays on. What happens without voltage normalisation?
options: Nothing, power does not depend on voltage
The meter reports reactive power instead
Only the fridge is affected because it has a motor
Resistive loads draw more power, the aggregate steps up, and the edge detector may report a spurious event
explain: A resistive load draws power proportional to voltage squared, so every resistive appliance draws more and the total steps up with no appliance switching. Normalising to a nominal voltage removes that step, which is why Hart's pipeline normalises before edge detection.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: Which situation is deduplication rather than linking to a reference list?
options: Mapping job titles to O*NET-SOC occupation codes
Grouping company names scraped from resumes when no company registry is available
Mapping school names to a fixed list of accredited universities
explain: With a reference list, each string is matched to an existing entry. Without one, you must discover the groups themselves and mint IDs for them, which is deduplication. Both use cleaning, blocking and pairwise scoring.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: A raw title `Sr SDET` must map to an O*NET code. Which pipeline gets it right in the computed example?
options: Embed the raw string and take the nearest occupation name
Lowercase, then exact lookup in the occupation names
Expand abbreviations, strip seniority, then match against occupation names plus alternate titles
Strip seniority only, then embed and take the nearest occupation name
explain: Raw abbreviations score near noise (`SDET` peaks at 0.25), and an exact lookup never finds `sr sdet`. Even after expansion, the occupation name alone picks Software Developers (0.68 vs 0.60). Matching against reported titles such as Software Test Engineer gives QA at 0.92.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: An ET server reads one 4096-byte chunk per event and then returns to epoll_wait. A client uploads 10,000 bytes in one burst and waits for a reply. What happens?
options: The server reads all 10,000 bytes over three wakeups
epoll_wait returns EAGAIN
The kernel splits the burst into three separate edge events
The server reads 4096 bytes and may never be woken for the remaining 5904, so the client hangs
explain: Once all the bytes are queued, nothing new arrives after the first 4096 are read, so there is no new edge, and epoll_wait can block forever with 5904 bytes in the buffer. This is exactly step 5 of the epoll(7) example. Fix: read until EAGAIN, or until a short read on a stream socket.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Your team trains a learned reranker on click logs from January to June and evaluates on 300 labeled queries sampled from the same months. Which leak is most likely to inflate the test score?
options: The test queries use graded rather than binary labels
Many test queries, or close paraphrases of them, also appear in the training clicks
The test set is too large for a bootstrap confidence interval
The reranker uses a cross-encoder instead of a bi-encoder
explain: Popular queries repeat. A reranker trained on clicks for a query has effectively seen its answer. Split by query cluster and preferably by time (train on earlier months, test on later), so test queries are genuinely new.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Which access pattern causes the most coherence traffic on one 64-byte line?
options: Eight threads each read a different 8-byte field
One thread repeatedly writes all eight fields
Two threads on different cores each write their own field
Eight threads read the same field
explain: Reads leave the line Shared in every cache with no ongoing traffic. A single writer keeps the line Modified in its own cache with no one to invalidate. Two writers on different cores each need an RFO before each write after the other one wrote, so the line ping-pongs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: Eight hospitals want one shared model and no record may leave any hospital. What is the training objective?
options: Each hospital trains alone and the best of the eight models is shipped
The same pooled average loss as centralized training, written as a sum of per-hospital losses weighted by record count
The unweighted mean of the eight per-hospital losses, since each hospital is one client
A new objective that no centralized training run could express
explain: Federated learning changes who computes, not what is being minimized. The objective is the pooled average loss, which factors exactly into a sum over clients with weights n_k/n. The unweighted mean is a different objective: it would give a hospital with 200 records the same influence as one with 20000.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
question: You need 200 reporting devices per round and measure an 8 percent dropout rate. How many should you invite, and what happens to the extras?
options: Exactly 200, and retry the ones that fail inside the same round
About 260 (130 percent), closing the round once 200 have reported and aborting the rest
As many as check in, aggregating every update that ever arrives
400, so that a full round survives even if half the devices vanish
explain: Over-selecting by about 130 percent is the deployed practice: it absorbs the 6 to 10 percent that drop out and lets the slowest tail be discarded. The round closes on the quorum, and the surplus tail gets aborted, which is why 22 percent of sessions in the measured population finished training but had their result rejected.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: A team has an existing HNSW index over 500M vectors and cannot afford a long rebuild. Which approach fits best?
options: ACORN-gamma with gamma = 1/s_min
ACORN-1 style two-hop lookups over a standard HNSW-like graph
StitchedVamana with one graph per label
Raise M in the existing HNSW and rebuild
explain: ACORN-1 needs no expanded lists at build time; it reconstructs a denser neighborhood during search. Weaviate took this route: its blog says it kept vanilla HNSW indexing so existing data does not need re-indexing. ACORN-gamma and StitchedVamana both require heavier construction, and raising M flattens the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
question: Why does Algorithm 1 use sign(e) rather than e itself?
options: The paper tried b += u x e and found it slightly better balanced but no better in perplexity, so it kept the simpler sign rule
sign(e) is required for causality
Using e would make the bias receive gradients
sign(e) guarantees exact balance every step
explain: Table 3 of the paper compares variants: the proportional rule reached MaxVio 0.028 to 0.040 with perplexity 9.51 to 9.53, versus 0.044 and 9.50 for the sign rule with u = 0.001. Neither variant involves gradients or future tokens.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
question: Why does multiplying both Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix reduce FP8 error without changing the attention output?
options: It shrinks every value toward zero, so rounding errors are smaller
Scores are preserved because $MM^\top = I$, and mixing entries spreads outliers so one scale fits all entries better
It sorts the head dimension so outliers end up in a single block that is kept in FP16
It converts the values to integers, which FP8 represents exactly
explain: Orthogonality keeps $QK^\top$ identical. Each rotated entry is a signed sum of many original entries, which evens out magnitudes (max/RMS fell from 1.99 to 1.07 in the toy example), so quantization with a shared scale loses less information.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
question: A request has exactly 8 tokens in a cache with page_size 4. What are its page count and kv_last_page_len?
options: 3 pages, last_page_len 0
2 pages, last_page_len 0
2 pages, last_page_len 4
3 pages, last_page_len 4
explain: 8 tokens fill exactly 2 pages. The docs require $1 \le$ last_page_len $\le$ page_size, and the length formula gives $4 \cdot (2 - 1) + 4 = 8$. Writing 0 would describe a 4-token request; adding an empty third page wastes a whole page and breaks the formula.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: Why does FlashInfer pick a different query tile for decode than for long prefill instead of always using a large one?
options: Large tiles give wrong results for decode
A decode query has few rows, so a 128-row tile would be mostly padding and waste compute and shared memory
Small tiles have higher arithmetic intensity
Tile size must equal the page size
explain: Tile size affects efficiency, not correctness. With 1 to a few fused rows per request, a 128-row tile spends almost all of its work on empty rows. The paper notes the usual FA2 tile is good for prefill on A100 but inefficient for decode. Page size is independent of the query tile.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Your codebase follows SD3: $z_t = (1-t)x_0 + t\epsilon$ with $x_0$ data. A colleague plugs in a rectified flow sampler that starts at $t=0$ from noise and adds $h \cdot v$. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, the conventions are identical
Only the step size needs to double
It starts from noise at the data end of time and steps in the wrong direction; it must start at t = 1 and integrate toward t = 0 (subtracting h times the predicted velocity)
It works but needs logit-normal sampling at inference
explain: Under SD3's convention noise lives at t = 1 and the network predicts the velocity toward noise, epsilon - x0. Sampling must run t from 1 down to 0, i.e. z goes to z - h v. Mixing conventions silently produces garbage.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Model checking a consensus core: votes, quorums and restarts
question: Your team proposes a Raft optimization: reply to RequestVote first and write votedFor to disk asynchronously. How would you use the spec?
options: Skip modeling; the change only affects latency
Model the reply and the disk write as separate actions, with a crash that can fall between them, and rerun TLC
Increase the number of values to 10 and check again unchanged
Prove it with Verus because TLA+ cannot model disks
explain: Splitting one atomic step into two creates new interleavings, here a crash after the reply but before the write. That window is exactly the Restart bug, and TLC will find it. AWS describes using specs this way to check that deep changes are safe before shipping.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scales are stale; switch to delayed scaling
Too few mantissa bits in the inputs; switch all inputs to E5M2
Limited-precision accumulation inside the tensor cores; promote partial sums to FP32 every N_C elements
The output is BF16; write it in FP8 instead
explain: The DeepSeek report traces large-K error to about 14-bit accumulation in Hopper FP8 tensor cores and fixes it by moving partial sums to FP32 on CUDA cores every 128 elements. E5M2 inputs would make precision worse, not better.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
question: Spot the bug. A program writes `state.tmp`, calls `rename("state.tmp", "state")`, then fsyncs the directory. It never fsyncs `state.tmp`. What can a crash leave behind?
options: Nothing bad: the directory fsync also flushes every file in it
Two files named state
A durable name `state` that points to a file whose new data never reached disk, so it may be empty or partial
The old `state` file, always, because rename is atomic
explain: The directory fsync makes the rename durable, but it does not flush the data of the files it names. Without an fsync of the temporary file before the rename, the name can survive while the contents do not. Atomic rename only protects what other processes see while the system is running.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
question: A search box accepts any dictionary word within 2 Levenshtein edits of the query. For which query is this rule most likely to return junk?
options: `cat` (3 letters)
`restaurant` (10 letters)
`levenshtein` (11 letters)
All three are equally safe because the threshold is the same
explain: Two edits can rewrite 2 of the 3 letters of `cat`, so `cut`, `bag`, `act` and many other 3-letter words all match. For a 10 or 11 letter word, 2 edits keep most of the string intact. This is why search engines scale the allowed edits with term length (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
question: In a BK-tree, the query is at distance 3 from a node and the search radius is 1. Which child subtrees are searched?
options: Only the child labelled 3
Children labelled 2, 3 and 4
Children labelled 0 to 4
All children, because 3 > 1
explain: Any match $u$ in a child labelled $i$ has $d(u,\text{node}) = i$ and $d(q,u) \le 1$, so by the triangle inequality $|i-3| \le 1$, giving $i \in \{2,3,4\}$. Every other child provably contains no match.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
question: A quad's code is (0.30, 0.40, 0.90, 0.20). What is the code of the same four stars if the labels A and B had been swapped?
explain: Swapping A and B turns the frame 180 degrees about (0.5, 0.5), so every coordinate becomes 1 minus itself. Here the original has xC + xD = 1.2 > 1 and the swapped one 0.8, so the canonical labeling is the swapped one (then C and D trade places to get xC <= xD).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: Groth's triangle matcher discards matched triangle pairs whose log perimeter ratio is far from the average. Why does that remove false matches?
options: False matches have larger perimeters
All true matches share one magnification between the lists, so their log perimeter ratios cluster, while false matches scatter
The perimeter is not scale invariant
It removes triangles with clockwise orientation
explain: Between two lists there is a single scale factor. Every truly corresponding triangle shows the same perimeter ratio; coincidental shape matches come from unrelated triangles of any size, so their ratios spread out. The same idea appears in Astrometry.net's scale-range check.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: How many cells does H3 resolution 2 have in total?
explain: c(r) = 2 + 120 x 7^r, so c(2) = 2 + 120 x 49 = 5,882. 122 is resolution 0 and 842 is resolution 1. The 12 pentagons are included in the count.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: A 5-tap filter on the row 10, 40, 90, 160 needs index -1 while computing output 0. Which rule returns 40 there?
options: REPLICATE
WRAP
REFLECT
REFLECT101
explain: REFLECT101 mirrors without repeating the edge, so index -1 maps to index 1, whose value is 40. REPLICATE clamps to index 0 and gives 10, REFLECT repeats the edge so it also gives 10, and WRAP folds to index 3, or 160. Only REFLECT101 reaches past the edge pixel to a real neighbour.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: You call torch.cuda.empty_cache() while a 3 MiB tensor is alive in a 20 MiB segment. How much of that segment is returned to the driver?
options: All 20 MiB, because only 3 MiB is in use
17 MiB, the free part
None of it, because the segment is split around a live block
3 MiB, the live tensor is moved to the small pool
explain: The allocator can only cudaFree a whole segment, and only when no block in it is in use. A partly used segment keeps all of its memory reserved, including the free 17 MiB.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: A training job OOMs. memory_allocated is 30 GB, memory_reserved is 39 GB on a 40 GB GPU, and memory_summary shows 8 GB of inactive split blocks. What should you try first?
options: Enable expandable_segments to avoid stranded slivers in fixed segments
Call empty_cache() before every step
Switch to a smaller block size for the KV cache
Lower garbage_collection_threshold to 0.1
explain: 8 GB free inside split segments is fragmentation, which empty_cache cannot release because those segments hold live tensors. Expandable segments target exactly that; max_split_size_mb is the documented fallback.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: All 32 threads of a warp read `s[7]` from a shared float array. How many passes does the access need?
options: 32, because every thread uses bank 7
16, because pairs of threads share a pass
1, because the word is broadcast
2, because reads of one bank are paired
explain: A bank conflict needs different addresses in the same bank. Here every thread asks for the same word, which the hardware broadcasts in a single pass.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
question: After rewriting a kernel it runs in 0.62 ms instead of 0.90 ms, but its Memory Throughput row fell from 48 percent to 41 percent. What do you conclude?
options: The rewrite is a regression: the kernel now uses the memory system less efficiently
The measurement must be wrong, since less time with the same work implies a higher percent of peak
The rewrite is a 1.45x win; a SOL row can fall when the work itself shrinks, and duration is the thing you validate against
Nothing can be concluded without re-running with cache control disabled
explain: If the rewrite removed traffic, for example by fusing a pass or improving reuse, the kernel moves fewer bytes in less time, and the percent of peak can fall while the duration improves. The triage guide says to validate every change against absolute kernel duration for exactly this reason. The percentages are for classification, not scoring.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
question: A block of 256 threads executes `if (threadIdx.x < 96) heavy(); else light();`. How many of its 8 warps diverge on this branch?
options: 0: 96 is a multiple of 32, so the split falls on a warp boundary
3: warps 0 to 2 run heavy()
8: any if statement makes every warp run both paths
1: only the warp containing thread 96
explain: Threads 0 to 95 are exactly warps 0, 1 and 2; threads 96 to 255 are warps 3 to 7. Every warp's 32 threads agree, so no warp has to run both paths. Divergence is a per-warp property, not a per-block one.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Why does increasing k (retrieving more chunks) not solve global questions on a 1-million-token corpus?
options: Because embeddings cannot represent questions
Because LLMs cannot read more than 10 chunks
Because chunks overlap by 100 tokens
Because the retrieved set is still ranked by similarity to the question and bounded by the context window, so it is a biased sample, not the whole corpus
explain: Retrieval chooses what is similar to the question words, and the context window caps how much fits. For "main themes" the relevant evidence is everywhere, so any top-k set is a sample presented as if it were a global view.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
question: Your corpus doubles from 1M to 2M tokens with the same settings. Roughly what happens to extraction LLM calls?
options: They stay the same because the graph is reused
They roughly double, because extraction runs once per chunk
They grow quadratically with the number of entity pairs
They halve because chunks get larger
explain: Extraction is one prompt (plus gleaning) per chunk, so it scales linearly with the number of chunks. Summaries and reports depend on graph size, which also tends to grow.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
question: A group of 4 answers gets rewards 1, 0, 1, 0. Using the population std, what is the advantage of each correct answer?
explain: Mean 0.5, population std 0.5, so (1 - 0.5) / 0.5 = +1.0. Wrong answers get -1.0.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
question: Your app needs the scheduled arrival time of trip T1 at stop S3. Which tables must you read?
options: routes.txt and stops.txt
trips.txt and calendar.txt
stop_times.txt, filtered by trip_id = T1 and stop_id or stop_sequence
frequencies.txt, because every trip has a headway
explain: Times live only in stop_times.txt, one row per (trip_id, stop_sequence). trips.txt names the route and service but has no times. frequencies.txt is optional and only used for headway-based or compressed trips.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
question: Your poller sees header timestamps 08:10:30, then 08:10:00, then 08:11:00 from a feed behind a load balancer. What should it do with the 08:10:00 message?
options: Apply it, because the newest download always wins
Merge it with the 08:10:30 message entity by entity
Ignore it and keep the 08:10:30 state, since the timestamp went backwards
Stop polling, the feed is broken
explain: Best practices say the header timestamp should not decrease, and describe exactly this load balancer case. Keeping the newest state by timestamp avoids flicker between replicas.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
question: You sample cycles with `perf record -c 3000000` on a core running steadily at 3 GHz. The program uses 2 seconds of CPU time. About how many samples do you get?
explain: 2 s x 3 GHz = 6 billion cycles; one sample every 3 million cycles gives 2000 samples. The 4000 Hz default only applies with frequency mode, not with -c.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
question: A team sets nr_hugepages so the pool covers 90% of RAM "to be safe", and their app uses half of it. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: unused huge pages are lent to the page cache
The unused pool pages are unavailable to the page cache and other processes, so the rest of the system runs short of memory
The kernel converts unused huge pages back to 4 KiB pages after a minute
khugepaged splits the unused pages and swaps them
explain: Persistent pool pages are reserved inside the kernel and cannot be used for other purposes or swapped, per the HugeTLB docs. Only surplus pages (from nr_overcommit_hugepages) are returned when unused. The pool should be sized to what the application needs.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
question: In a Mamba-2 head, the model sees a token that marks the start of an unrelated document. What setting lets the head discard the old context?
options: A small step size dt, so a stays near 1
A large step size dt, so a falls toward 0
Setting C to zero for that token
Increasing the state size N for that token
explain: a = exp(dt A) with A negative. A large dt drives a toward 0, which multiplies the whole state by a small number. C only affects what is read, and N is fixed by the architecture.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
