lessonTitle: Why BM25 and dense retrieval miss different documents
question: A user searches a product catalog for the part number `XJ-4471B`. Which retriever is most likely to put the exact part page first, and why?
options: BM25, because the rare exact token gets a high IDF weight and the embedding may map similar part numbers close together
Dense retrieval, because embeddings capture meaning better than words
Neither; part numbers must be handled by a separate database
Both equally, since both see the same query text
explain: A rare identifier is exactly what BM25's IDF rewards: few documents contain it, so a match scores high. An embedding model has no reason to keep XJ-4471B far from XJ-4471C. This is the class of query where hybrid search keeps the lexical side.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
question: In HyDE, which component is trained or fine-tuned for the target task?
options: The Contriever encoder is fine-tuned on the generated passages
Nothing: both the LLM and the encoder are used as-is, only the instruction changes per task
The LLM is fine-tuned to write passages for the corpus
A small adapter maps query vectors to document vectors
explain: The paper states that no model is trained in HyDE. The only supervision anywhere is the instruction tuning the LLM already received. Adapting to SciFact or FiQA means writing a different instruction.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Why change detection must align images first
question: How many point pairs, at minimum, does an affine fit need?
explain: An affine transform has 6 DOF and each point pair supplies 2 equations, so 3 pairs (not collinear) determine it. 6 is the number of parameters, not of pairs; 4 is the minimum for a homography.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
question: The second image is uniformly brighter (gain and offset) and also contains a large new object covering 30 percent of the frame. Which photometric correction is most trustworthy?
options: Match global mean and standard deviation of the whole image
Skip correction and lower the threshold
Convert both images to binary before differencing
Fit gain and offset on pixels outside a first-pass change mask
explain: Global statistics include the new object, which shifts the mean and inflates the variance, so the correction is biased in proportion to how much changed. Estimating the photometric model from likely unchanged pixels avoids that, which is what the two-pass approach does in the toy.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
question: Your app writes 4 blocks then needs an fsync, while unrelated reads stream through the same ring. Which option keeps the 4 writes parallel and never stalls the unrelated reads?
options: Set IOSQE_IO_DRAIN on the fsync
Link write 1 to write 2 to write 3 to write 4 to fsync with IOSQE_IO_LINK
Submit the 4 writes, wait for their 4 CQEs, then submit the fsync (or use a separate ring for integrity writes)
Set IOSQE_ASYNC on the fsync
explain: A drain stalls everything else in the ring, and a link chain serializes the writes. Waiting for the 4 write CQEs before submitting the fsync keeps the writes parallel and leaves the other traffic alone. The paper also suggests a separate ring for integrity writes if drains are frequent.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: tcmalloc: rseq per-CPU caches, spans and Temeraire
question: Temeraire's filler has hugepage P with a 50-page free range and hugepage Q with a 3-page free range. A 2-page request arrives. Where does it go and why?
options: P, because it has the most free space
A fresh hugepage, to avoid fragmentation
Q, because it is the tightest fit, which keeps P's long range available for large requests
Whichever was used most recently
explain: The filler allocates from the hugepage with the smallest longest-free-range that fits. Placing small requests on P would break up its 50-page run, and a later large request would then need a new hugepage.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
question: A history contains write 5 (ok, 0 to 1 ms), then read (ok, 2 to 3 ms) returning 5, then write 6 (info, from 4 ms), then read (ok, 9 to 10 ms) returning 5. Is it linearizable?
options: No: write 6 was invoked, so the later read must see 6
Yes: the info write 6 may never have taken effect, or may take effect after 10 ms
No: two reads can never return the same value
It cannot be decided without the server logs
explain: An info operation may or may not take effect, and if it does, its point can lie anywhere after its invocation, including after the final read. So write 5, read 5, read 5 (with write 6 omitted or last) is a legal order.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
question: A kernel is tuned once at M = 4096 and the winner is cached under the key ['N', 'K'] only. Production then sends M = 16 requests. What is the most likely result?
options: Wrong numerical results, because the tile no longer covers the rows
A cache miss, because M changed
Correct results at a small fraction of achievable throughput, with no miss and no re-tune
A compile error, because the tile is larger than M
explain: Masking keeps the result correct and the kernel compiles fine. The key simply does not mention M, so the cache hits and reuses a configuration whose tile is eight times taller than the problem. In the model of this lesson that configuration retains about 0.21 of what the right one would achieve.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
question: You bind the NVMe SSD that holds a mounted /data filesystem to vfio-pci so an SPDK app can use it. What happens to /data?
options: It keeps working; SPDK and the kernel share the drive
The kernel loses the device: /dev/nvme0n1 disappears and the filesystem on it is gone from the kernel's view
It becomes read-only until SPDK exits
SPDK mounts it in user space automatically
explain: Unbinding removes the kernel driver, so the block device and everything built on it vanish. SPDK provides its own user-space storage layers, but not the kernel filesystem you had mounted.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
question: A firewall appliance must filter 40 Mpps of mostly small packets, but operators also need SSH and normal monitoring on the same 100 Gbit/s port. Which design fits best?
options: Kernel stack with larger socket buffers
Full vfio-pci bypass and a hand-written SSH server inside the DPDK app
Interrupt-mode DPDK with 8192-entry rings
A bifurcated driver (or flow bifurcation) so the data plane runs in DPDK and control traffic stays with the kernel
explain: Flow bifurcation lets NIC hardware steer data-plane flows to the PMD and the rest to Linux, keeping kernel tools. Full bypass would remove the kernel's view of the port; huge rings only add latency.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: In the PyTorch 2 ablation, disabling both fusion and inlining made compiled models slower than eager. Why?
options: torch.compile adds Python overhead per op
Inductor decomposes large operators into many primitives and relies on fusion to recombine them
Triton kernels are slower than CUDA kernels
Graph breaks increase without fusion
explain: The paper explains that decompositions break large optimized operators into smaller primitive ops, and fusion recombines them. Without fusion and inlining each primitive becomes its own kernel with its own HBM round trip, so the result is slower than eager's hand-written kernels.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: tokens, sequences, on-policy
question: A student fine-tuned on teacher-written answers does well on short replies but drifts into nonsense on long ones, while the teacher stays on track. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Raise the softmax temperature to 10
Switch from KL divergence to mean squared error on probabilities
Remove the hard-label loss
Train on the student's own sampled continuations with teacher token-level feedback (on-policy distillation)
explain: The symptom is compounding error from train-inference mismatch: the student never trained on its own imperfect prefixes. On-policy distillation (GKD, MiniLLM) samples from the student and asks the teacher what it should have done at each of those prefixes.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
question: In GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, what does each KV head serve?
options: A group of 4 query heads
One query head; the other 24 are unused
All 32 query heads
8 consecutive tokens
explain: Query heads are split into 8 groups of 4, and each group shares one key head and one value head.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
question: Why does PyramidKV give lower layers a bigger budget?
options: Lower layers have more heads
Higher layers are skipped at inference time
Lower layers use FP8 already
Attention in lower layers is spread over many tokens, while higher layers focus on a few
explain: Its analysis shows information funneling: broad attention low, concentrated attention high. Uniform budgets waste slots in high layers and starve low ones.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
question: In SGLang HiCache with the best_effort prefetch policy, a 4,000-token L3 hit is only half fetched when the GPU becomes free. What happens?
options: The fetched part is used with the local hits and the rest is computed by prefill
The request waits until all 4,000 tokens arrive
The partial prefetch is discarded and everything is recomputed
The request is moved to another instance that has the data in L2
explain: best_effort terminates prefetching as soon as the GPU can run prefill. The data already fetched is used together with the local data, and the remaining tokens are prefilled. wait_complete would have waited for all of it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
question: A service has 2,000 stateless frontends that all write to a shared database, and wants timestamps for snapshot reads. Why is a vector clock a poor fit?
options: Every timestamp and message would carry about 2,000 counters, and vectors still cannot express a physical time like 10:00
Vector clocks cannot be compared at all once there are more than 64 nodes
Vector clocks require synchronized physical clocks
Vector clocks only work with exactly three nodes
explain: Vector size grows with the number of participants, so each row version and each RPC would carry thousands of integers. Vector clocks also have no relation to wall time, so a snapshot "as of 10:00" is not expressible. This gap is what hybrid logical clocks target.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: MaxSim: each query token finds its best document token
question: You append 50 unrelated tokens (a cookie banner) to Doc A and re-encode. Ignoring small context shifts in the old tokens, what happens to its MaxSim score for this query?
options: It drops, because the score is normalized by document length
It stays the same or rises, because each row keeps its old maximum and can only find a higher one
It drops, because the extra tokens lower the average similarity
It doubles, because the matrix has more columns
explain: Each query row takes a max over document tokens. New columns can only tie or beat the old best match. This is why very long or noisy documents are usually split into passages before indexing.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
question: Which corpus is the strongest fit for ColPali over an OCR plus text-embedding pipeline?
options: 50,000 pages of financial reports full of charts and tables, where indexing speed matters
100 million short plain-text chat messages
A code search index over source files
A product catalog searched only by exact SKU
explain: ColPali's gains are largest on visually rich pages (infographics, figures, tables) and it skips slow OCR and captioning. Plain text at huge scale gains little from page images and pays heavily in storage; exact-match lookups need no neural retriever.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
question: Your team must ship a math tutor whose reasoning is reviewed by teachers for errors. Which approach fits best?
options: Coconut with 6 continuous thoughts, since it is faster
Pause tokens, since they need no CoT data
Written chain-of-thought, accepting the extra tokens, because reviewers need a readable trace
Recurrent depth with r = 64, since it has more effective layers
explain: Every latent method trades away a readable trace. When humans must audit the reasoning, written CoT is the only option here that provides one. It also had the highest GSM8k accuracy in Coconut's own table (42.9 vs 34.1).

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
question: You halve epsilon in a PGM-index over the same data. What do you expect?
options: Fewer segments and a faster last-mile search
More segments (more memory), a smaller search window per level, and possibly more levels
The same number of segments, because the optimal PLA does not depend on epsilon
Lookups become approximate
explain: A tighter error bound means each line covers fewer keys, so m grows (the bars show 72 segments at eps 64 versus 139 at eps 32 for log-normal keys). Each level's search window shrinks to 2 epsilon + 1, and the fan-out per level, at least 2 epsilon, shrinks too, so the tree can get deeper.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
question: A query expands to 40 non-zero terms, many of them common words with long posting lists. What happens to latency compared to a 6-term expansion?
options: Nothing; the dot product is computed on the GPU in constant time
It grows roughly with the total length of the touched posting lists, so it can get much slower
It shrinks, because more terms let WAND prune earlier
It depends only on the number of documents in the collection
explain: Term-at-a-time or document-at-a-time traversal reads every posting on every query term's list (minus what pruning skips). More and longer lists mean more work, which is why query sparsity is penalized harder.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
question: Query Q1 has 10 documents and query Q2 has 200, each with mixed labels. With an unnormalized pairwise loss, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because pairs are formed per query
Q1 dominates, because its pairs are more informative
Q2 dominates, because it can contribute vastly more pairs, so the loss stops tracking the per-query average NDCG
The model cannot be trained because pair counts differ
explain: Pair counts can grow quadratically with documents per query, so a few big queries dominate a pairwise loss. Liu describes query-level normalization (dividing by the query's pair count) as the fix; LightGBM's lambdarank_norm also normalizes per query.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
question: A linear-attention layer with $d_k=d_v=128$ per head has generated 10,000 tokens. What does it need to keep per head to generate token 10,001?
options: All 10,000 keys and values, like a KV cache
The 128 x 128 state matrix S
Only the last 128 keys
The full 10,000 x 10,000 attention matrix
explain: Everything the layer knows about the past is folded into $S_t$, a 128 x 128 matrix (16,384 numbers) regardless of how many tokens came before. That is the RNN view of linear attention.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise training and hybrid models in production
question: You must train a Gated DeltaNet layer on 8K-token sequences on GPUs. Which computation form should the training kernel use?
options: Recurrent form, because it has the fewest FLOPs
Fully parallel form, because it has no sequential steps
Chunkwise form, which keeps FLOPs near linear and turns most work into matmuls with only L/C sequential steps
Any form, they run equally fast
explain: The recurrent form serializes 8K small updates and cannot use tensor cores well; the parallel form pays $O(L^2d)$ FLOPs. Chunkwise is what FLA and the paper use for training.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
question: Per-topic tau in the TREC 2024 RAG study (0.553 for nDCG@20) is much lower than run-level tau (0.890). What does that tell you?
options: The LLM labels are useless
Run-level averages are wrong
LLM labels are noisy for any single query, so per-query diagnosis needs more care than leaderboard ranking
Per-topic tau is always lower because of a formula error
explain: Within one topic, label disagreements reorder runs a lot; averaged over 27 topics the noise cancels. Use LLM labels confidently for aggregate comparisons, cautiously for statements about a single query.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
question: Why does selective batching split the batch for attention but not for the QKV projection?
options: Attention has no weights, so batching it gains nothing and it must be skipped
The QKV projection runs on the CPU
Splitting the projection would require padding, splitting attention does not
Each token's projection uses only that token's row, but attention must combine a token only with earlier tokens of its own request
explain: A linear layer computes each output row from one input row, so the request a row belongs to is irrelevant and all rows share one weight read. Attention mixes rows, and mixing rows from different requests would be wrong, so it needs the boundaries (and each request's own past keys and values).

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
question: Which statement about the three engines is accurate according to their documentation?
options: All three swap preempted KV caches to CPU memory by default
SGLang keeps every running request's full max_new_tokens reserved until it finishes
vLLM V1 runs prefill and decode in separate scheduler queues with separate budgets
TensorRT-LLM's default capacity policy never pauses a request once started, while vLLM V1 recomputes preempted requests
explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT is TensorRT-LLM's default and guarantees started requests are not paused; vLLM V1 recomputes by default and removed CPU swapping for preemption. SGLang counts running requests' remaining tokens at an estimated ratio rather than their full maximum, and vLLM V1 uses one unified token budget.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
question: Why does the Outlines index map FSM states, rather than generated prefixes, to allowed tokens?
options: Prefixes are too short to be useful keys
There are finitely many states, each summarizing all prefixes that lead to it, so the table can be built once ahead of time
States are faster to hash than strings
The model's logits depend only on the FSM state
explain: Possible prefixes are unbounded, but the FSM has a fixed number of states, and any two prefixes that reach the same state allow exactly the same continuations. That is what makes ahead-of-time indexing possible. The logits still depend on the full prefix.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Ambiguity, negation and graceful fallback
question: Which parse is correct for *backend people who know java (not javascript) in hamburg*?
options: skills: [java], skills_not: [javascript]
skills: [java, javascript], skills_not: []
skills: [], skills_not: [java, javascript]
skills: [java], skills_not: [], text: not javascript
explain: Java is required and JavaScript is excluded. Option two is the dropped-negation error that appears in the lesson 5 set. Putting the exclusion in text makes it a scored match, which would actually boost profiles that mention JavaScript.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
question: PRP all-pairs at k=100 issues how many prompts, counting both orders?
explain: k(k-1) = 100 x 99 = 9,900: every unordered pair (4,950) in both orders.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: RankZephyr is distilled into 7B from GPT-4 orderings. Which cost quantity does distillation change?
options: The number of windows per query
The input tokens per window
The compute per token, plus access to batching, caching and logits when self-hosted
The number of output tokens per window
explain: Calls and tokens follow from k, w, s and L. Distillation shrinks the model, so each token costs less compute, and hosting it yourself unlocks the serving levers.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows
question: Which change most directly reduces the number of listwise calls for 100 candidates?
options: Shrinking the window from 20 to 10 at the same step of 10
Raising the step from 10 to 15 with w = 20 (overlap 5)
Running a second pass
Adding more few-shot examples
explain: Calls per pass are floor((M - w)/s) + 1. With s = 15: floor(80/15) + 1 = 6 instead of 9. The cost is a smaller overlap (only the best 5 passages are carried along), and since 15 does not divide 80, the last window covers ranks 6 to 25 and ranks 1 to 5 are never reranked. Shrinking w to 10 with s = 10 removes the overlap entirely, so passages could no longer travel between windows.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
question: Why does ORB rank FAST keypoints by the Harris measure?
options: FAST has no cornerness score and responds strongly along edges, so Harris picks the most corner-like points
Harris makes the detector scale invariant
Harris computes the orientation
Harris is needed to compute the Hamming distance
explain: The ORB paper says FAST produces no cornerness measure and has large responses along edges. Ordering by the Harris response and keeping the top N removes edge-like points. Scale comes from the pyramid and orientation from the intensity centroid.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
question: In `push`, T1's CAS fails. What does that tell T1?
options: Its node was lost and must be reallocated
Another thread's CAS on top succeeded since T1 read it, so the system made progress and T1 should relink and retry
The stack is full
A spurious failure always, because compare_exchange_weak never fails otherwise
explain: In this algorithm, top only changes through a successful CAS. If T1's CAS fails (ignoring rare spurious failures), some other push or pop completed. That is the lock-free argument in one sentence. T1's node is still private and simply gets relinked.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
question: A service uses epoch-based reclamation. One worker thread pins, then blocks on a slow network call while still pinned. What happens?
options: Nothing: EBR is lock-free
Other threads deadlock immediately
The global epoch stops advancing past one step beyond that thread's epoch, so retired memory grows without bound until it unpins
The stalled thread's reads become unsafe
explain: Advancement requires every pinned participant to be in the current epoch. The stalled thread is fine and other threads keep operating, but garbage bags can no longer age by 2 epochs, so memory grows. Keep pinned regions short and never block inside them.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
question: Your per-template counters show T2 done collapsing while T1 recv holds steady, and a brand new template T3 exc appearing. What does the pair of signals tell you that a single total-log-volume alert could not?
options: Nothing extra: total volume would have dropped too
Only that something changed, since template counts cannot be attributed to code paths
That work is still arriving but stopped completing, and a previously unseen code path is now executing, which localizes the fault to one logging statement and its callers
That the parser is drifting and the templates should be recomputed
explain: Total volume barely moves here: T1 is flat and T2's loss is partly replaced by T3's gain. Per-template series separate arrival from completion and surface the new error path. A new template id is the strongest single signal in log analytics, which is why it deserves its own first-seen rule rather than a z-score.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
question: A colleague implements YaRN by scaling queries by 1.2773 for s = 16 but forgets the keys. What is the effect on the logits?
options: Correct: the temperature is defined on queries only
Logits are unchanged because softmax is scale invariant
Logits are scaled by 1.2773 instead of the intended 1.6314
Logits are scaled by 1.6314 squared
explain: YaRN multiplies both rotated q and k (via cos and sin) by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln 16 + 1 = 1.2773, so the dot product is scaled by 1.2773 squared = 1.6314. Scaling only one side gives just 1.2773. Softmax is shift invariant, not scale invariant.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
question: On i-GSM, (1 x 8) scores 73.2%, (8 x 1) scores 73.2% and (1 x 1) scores 24.5%. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Looping only helps because it adds parameters
The task is limited by memorized knowledge, so parameters matter most
The task mainly needs sequential depth; parameters beyond one layer add little here
Looped models are always as good as deep models on every task
explain: The looped model has the parameters of (1 x 1) but matches (8 x 1), so what the extra layers provided was depth, not capacity. That does not generalize to every task: later in the course you will see that knowledge-heavy tasks do need parameters.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
question: For k = 8, Saunshi et al. report open-book QA scores of 33.9 (24 layers), 22.7 (8 layers) and 30.8 (8 layers looped 3x). What is the % Gap?
options: About 24%
About 51%
About 72%
About 136%
explain: (30.8 - 22.7) / (33.9 - 22.7) = 8.1 / 11.2 = 0.72, about 72%, matching the paper's table. The looped model recovers most of the missing parameters' benefit on this context-reasoning group.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: Unlearned model A uses a small learning rate plus a retain loss and keeps 95% of its utility. Model B used plain gradient ascent and collapsed to near-zero utility. After 4-bit quantization, which is more likely to reveal the forgotten knowledge again?
options: A, because its small weight changes mostly fall inside the same quantization bins as the original weights
B, because gradient ascent changes few weights
Neither, quantization only reduces precision and cannot restore information
Both equally, quantization resets every model to the original
explain: Quantization maps every weight within half a step of a grid point to the same value. Utility-preserving unlearning moves weights by tiny amounts, so the quantized unlearned model is nearly the quantized original, which still knows the facts. Zhang et al. saw 21% retained knowledge rise to 83% at 4 bits; GA was the exception only because it had wrecked the model.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
question: In the 64-objects-per-page model, a workload frees 95% of its objects at random. What fraction of pages becomes returnable?
options: About 95%
About 3.8%
About 50%
Exactly 0%
explain: A page is empty only if all 64 objects died: 0.95^64 is about 0.0375, so about 3.8% of pages. The other 96% each hold at least one survivor and stay resident. Correlated lifetimes in real programs do better than this random model.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
question: A spin lock is implemented as `while LOCKED.swap(true, Acquire) {}` ... critical section ... `LOCKED.store(false, ORD)`. Which ORD is the weakest correct choice?
options: Relaxed
Acquire
SeqCst, because unlocking must be globally visible
Release
explain: The unlock must publish the critical section's writes to the next locker. That needs a Release store paired with the Acquire swap. Acquire is not even allowed on a plain store, Relaxed creates no happens-before, and SeqCst works but promises far more than needed.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: A developer removes the re-validation step: after `hp[me] = t; full_fence();` the code reads `t->next` directly. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the fence already makes the hazard pointer visible
Another thread may have retired and freed t before the hazard pointer was published, so reading its next field touches freed memory
The CAS will always fail
The retired list will grow without bound
explain: Publishing only protects a node that is still in the structure at the moment the slot becomes visible. If t was unlinked and a scan ran between the load and the publish, the scan saw no slot and freed t. The re-read proves t was still reachable after the publish, so every later scan must see the slot.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A Rust program uses crossbeam-epoch. Memory grows steadily, and a profiler shows one thread blocked on a channel receive inside a function that holds an `epoch::Guard`. What fixes it?
options: Increase the bag size from 64
Drop the guard (or call repin) before blocking on the channel
Switch the CAS to SeqCst ordering
Call `pin()` more often on other threads
explain: The blocked thread stays pinned in an old epoch, so the global epoch cannot advance past it and every thread's garbage waits. Bag size and memory ordering do not change that. Holding guards only for short, non-blocking sections is the rule for any grace-period scheme.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: System X ranks a query's 10 true matches at positions 1, 40, 41, ..., 48. System Y ranks them at positions 2 to 11. Which statement is right?
options: X has the better rank-1 and the better AP
Both have the same AP because both find all 10 matches
Y has the better rank-1, X the better AP
X has the better rank-1, but Y has a much better AP
explain: X's first match is at position 1, so rank-1 is a hit for X and a miss for Y. But X buries 9 matches around position 40, so its precision at those hits is low. AP is about 0.22 for X and 0.80 for Y. AP rewards finding all instances early, which is why Market-1501 reports mAP.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
question: Version X averages 102 ns with 95% interval [98, 106]. Version Y averages 100 ns with interval [97, 103]. What should you conclude?
options: Y is 2% faster; ship it
X is faster because its interval is wider
Compare the fastest runs instead
The data do not show a difference; reduce noise or take more runs before deciding
explain: The intervals overlap heavily, so a 2 ns gap is within what noise produces. Width says how uncertain the mean is, not which version is faster. The best-of approach is the misleading method that Georges et al. warn against.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
question: A token has rollout logprob -2.30 and trainer logprob -1.40, so r is about 2.46. What weight does it get under TIS with the default interval, and under clip-or-pop?
options: TIS 2.46, clip-or-pop 2.0
TIS 1.0, clip-or-pop 0
TIS 2.0, clip-or-pop 0
TIS 0, clip-or-pop 2.0
explain: TIS clamps r to [0, 2] and keeps the clamped value, so the token is damped to 2.0. Clip-or-pop zeroes the weight of any token outside the interval, so it is dropped. Tokens inside the interval keep their unclipped r under both.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
question: Spot the bug: to save build time, a team computes each leaf's min and max error on a 10% random sample of its keys, then searches only that window at lookup time.
options: Nothing breaks; sampling only makes the bounds slightly loose
Lookups get slower but always remain correct
Some stored keys can fall outside the window and lookups for them will wrongly report not found
The routing in stage 0 stops working
explain: The guarantee comes from checking every stored key. A key outside the sample can have a larger error than any sampled key, so a search limited to the window misses it. Either compute bounds on all keys (one pass, cheap) or search outward with exponential search, which needs no bounds.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
question: Why didn't DeepSeek simply use MQA, which has an even smaller cache than MLA?
options: MQA cannot be used with a KV cache
In their 7B ablation MQA lost clearly to MHA on hard benchmarks, and they wanted MHA-level quality
MQA needs more GPU memory for weights
MQA does not support causal masking
explain: DeepSeek-V2 Appendix D.1 shows MQA at 37.9 MMLU vs 45.2 for MHA at 7B. MLA was designed to get a small cache without paying that quality cost.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
question: For a long prompt's prefill, why does vLLM up-project the latents into full keys and values instead of using the absorbed path?
options: The absorbed path gives different numerical results
Prefill does not use a KV cache
Prefill is compute-bound, and the absorbed path does more FLOPs per score (576-wide vs 192-wide dot products), while its memory savings matter little there
RoPE cannot be applied during prefill
explain: Both paths compute the same function. The absorbed form wins when reading the cache dominates (decode); the plain multi-head form wins when arithmetic dominates (prefill).

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: How N trades recall against latency and cost
question: Using the simplified model with p = 0.4, which change helps recall more at N = 4: making phrasings less similar (rho from 0.8 to 0.5) or adding four more similar phrasings (N = 8 at rho = 0.8)?
options: Adding four more similar phrasings
Both give exactly the same recall
Making phrasings less similar
Neither changes recall
explain: At rho = 0.5, N = 4 gives 0.693. At rho = 0.8, N = 8 gives 0.665, with twice the searches. Diverse phrasings beat more of the same.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
question: In the MaxSim toy, you append five more unrelated tokens to doc A. What happens to A's MaxSim score?
options: It drops, because the average similarity falls
It rises, because more tokens means more matches
It is unchanged unless a new token beats an existing best match
It becomes undefined because A is longer than the query
explain: MaxSim takes, for each query token, the maximum over document tokens. Extra tokens can only raise a maximum, never lower it, and unrelated ones (low cosine) leave the maxima at 0.99, 1.00, 1.00. Mean pooling, in contrast, is diluted by them.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Shared trunk, n heads, and the memory trick that keeps it cheap
question: A colleague implements MTP with n = 4 by summing four head losses and calling backward once. Training now runs out of memory at the old batch size. What is the most likely cause?
options: The trunk activations are stored four times
All four heads' V-sized logits and gradients are alive at once, so peak memory grows with n
The shared unembedding matrix is copied four times
Cross-entropy needs fp64 when several losses are summed
explain: Summing losses and calling backward once keeps every head's logits in the graph until the end, so logit memory scales as nV per token. Running forward and backward per head and accumulating the d-sized gradient at the trunk keeps only one head's logits alive.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
question: An update has singular values 4.00, 1.00, 0.197 and 0.0019. What does replacing it with its orthogonalized version $UV^\top$ do?
options: Shrinks every entry toward zero, like weight decay
Keeps only the top direction and discards the rest
Keeps the same singular directions but sets every singular value to 1, boosting the weak directions relative to the strong one
Makes the update elementwise plus or minus 1, exactly like sign descent
explain: $UV^\top$ keeps $U$ and $V$ (the directions) and replaces $S$ with the identity. The strongest direction is scaled down from 4.00 to 1 and the weakest is scaled up from 0.0019 to 1. Sign descent is a different, elementwise operation, and as we saw it gives singular values 3.24, 2.00, 1.24, 0.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs, distributing it, and choosing an optimizer
question: A team adds Muon to *every* 2D parameter, including the token embedding and the LM head, and sees worse loss than their Muon-plus-AdamW baseline. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Newton-Schulz in bf16 is inaccurate for very wide matrices
Muon cannot handle matrices with more rows than columns
The embedding and output layers train better with AdamW; Muon is meant for hidden-layer matrices
They forgot to normalize by the Frobenius norm
explain: Both the Muon post and the reference implementation say input and output layers should use AdamW even though they are 2D. The post links the embedding's different dynamics to modular-norm theory and calls the head's preference for AdamW empirical. Nothing is wrong with the Newton-Schulz math itself.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
question: A team tunes a width-256 muP proxy, then launches the 4096-wide target with the same HPs but builds it with plain `nn.Linear` output and `torch.optim.AdamW`. What should they expect?
options: Identical results, since the HPs are the same
Behaviour like naive SP transfer: logits that grow with width and a learning rate that is too large for hidden layers, often divergence
Better results, since SP is more flexible
Slower but stable training
explain: The tuned numbers only mean something inside muP. Without the 1/m logit multiplier and the 1/m hidden Adam LR, the target is an SP model with a proxy-sized learning rate, which is exactly the naive transfer that diverged in the paper's IWSLT, WMT and BERT experiments.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
question: Why does FUTEX_WAIT take an expected value at all, instead of simply sleeping?
options: To pick which waiter FUTEX_WAKE will wake
To set the futex word to that value before sleeping
So a wake-up that happened after the caller's check but before it was queued is not lost
So the kernel can store the lock state between calls
explain: The waiter decided to sleep based on an earlier load. If an unlock and wake happened after that load, the word has changed, and the atomic compare in FUTEX_WAIT catches it. The kernel never stores the lock state; it just compares.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
question: A Repeatable Read transaction only runs plain SELECT statements (no FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE). Can it fail with a serialization error in PostgreSQL?
options: Yes, whenever another transaction updates a row it read
No, the docs say read-only Repeatable Read transactions never have serialization conflicts
Yes, if it reads more than one table
Only if it runs longer than the statement timeout
explain: The 40001 at Repeatable Read comes from trying to modify or lock a row changed after the snapshot. A transaction that only reads never does that, so it never needs a retry at this level.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
question: What does the reduction to per-token labelling buy you?
options: It removes the need for a decoder, since the labels are already the spans
It lets the model predict overlapping entities
It guarantees the predicted spans are always valid
It turns an unbounded structured output into one fixed-size classification per position, which any classifier can emit
explain: One label per token is a fixed-size decision per position, which any classifier can emit. You still need a decoder, the output can still be an invalid tag sequence, and a single chain of labels cannot represent overlapping spans at all.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
question: In the Hugging Face recipe, why do continuation sub-pieces get -100 rather than the word's label?
options: Because -100 is a reserved label id for the O class
Because the loss would otherwise be dominated by long words
Because the tokenizer cannot tell which word a continuation piece belongs to
Because the classifier is trained and read out on the first piece of each word, so the other pieces must be excluded from the loss
explain: -100 is the ignore index of PyTorch's cross-entropy, not a class. The convention is one prediction per word, taken at the word's first piece, exactly as the BERT paper describes, so every other piece must be masked out of the loss.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
question: Why does NSA select contiguous blocks of 64 tokens instead of the 1024 individually highest-scoring tokens?
options: Individual tokens cannot be scored
Blocks need less KV cache storage
Token-level selection is not allowed with softmax
Contiguous blocks give coalesced memory loads and Tensor Core tiles, and attention scores tend to be spatially clustered anyway
explain: GPUs read contiguous memory far faster than scattered indices, and tensor-core matrix multiplies want tiles. The paper also shows attention is blockwise clustered, so blocks lose little. DSA (lesson 5) does select individual tokens, but needs a different kernel design and a separately trained indexer to score them.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
question: Why does Krawetz's pHash leave the DC term out of the mean it thresholds against?
options: Because the DC term is usually far larger than the other coefficients and would distort the average, and it only encodes overall brightness
Because the DC term is always negative
Because the DCT does not define a DC term
To make the hash 63 bits instead of 64
explain: The DC term is the flat component, the overall brightness. In the toy it is 25804 while the next largest magnitude is 3491; including it in a mean would drag the threshold upward. Krawetz quotes pHash author David Starkweather: leaving it out excludes flat color information from the hash.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
question: A teammate wants to move a GRPO run from 1 GPU to 64 GPUs. Which part should not need to change?
options: The cluster section of the YAML config
The resource reservation made by RayVirtualCluster
The body of the grpo_train loop
The number of worker processes in each RayWorkerGroup
explain: The loop calls interfaces such as generate, get_logprobs and train. Scaling changes the cluster config, the placement groups and the number of workers, but the controller logic stays the same.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running the GRPO math example and reading its config
question: A group of 4 rollouts has rewards [1, 1, 1, 0]. With the default leave-one-out and normalization settings, what advantage does the wrong rollout get?
options: -1.0, because its three peers are all 1 so the division is skipped
explain: Its peers [1, 1, 1] are identical, so b = 1 and NeMo RL skips the std division: A = 0 - 1 = -1.0. Each correct rollout sees [1, 1, 0], mean 0.667 and sample std 0.577, so A = 0.333 / 0.577 = 0.577.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
question: In the model, the interconnect is upgraded to 80 GiB/s per direction. What is the new time for the interleave placement?
explain: Each link direction now carries 16 GiB at 80 GiB/s = 0.2 s, but each controller still needs 32 / 100 = 0.32 s. The maximum is 0.32 s, so interleave now matches parallel first touch in bandwidth (its misses are still slower on average).

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
question: A greedy cleaner finds that the best victim has 60 of its 64 pages valid. What is the write amplification of this cleaning cycle?
options: About 1.07
explain: It copies 60 pages to free 4. The flash writes 64 pages (60 copies plus 4 host pages) for 4 host pages: 64/4 = 16. This is what happens on a nearly full drive under random writes.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
question: A label file contains `0 0.5 0.5 0.2 0.4` for a 640 x 480 image in the Ultralytics YOLO format. What is the box width in pixels?
options: 0.2 px, the value is already in pixels
96 px
128 px
256 px
explain: YOLO labels are class, x_center, y_center, width, height, normalized by image size. Width 0.2 times the image width of 640 gives 128 px. Multiplying by the height (480) gives 96, a common mix-up.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
question: You must count about 3000 people in a single aerial photo of a festival crowd, where each head is a few pixels wide. Which approach fits best?
options: A detector with NMS at IoU 0.5, counting boxes
SORT tracking with line crossings
A density-map model such as CSRNet, summing the predicted map
Raising the detector's confidence threshold
explain: Tiny, overlapping heads are exactly where detection and NMS fail, and tracking needs video. A density model trained on dot annotations estimates the count by integrating the map, and regional sums still show where the crowd is densest.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
question: Which workload is the best fit for S3-native (diskless) rather than tiered Kafka?
options: Log and telemetry pipelines with high throughput, bursty load, and an end-to-end latency budget of about a second
Payment authorization needing 5 ms produce latency
A small cluster with 1 hour of retention and steady load
A compacted topic used as a key-value changelog with sub-millisecond reads
explain: S3-native systems acknowledge after a PUT and a metadata commit, so produce latency is hundreds of milliseconds, fine for telemetry but not a 5 ms payment path. Their payoff, stateless scaling and no cross-AZ replication, matters most for large, bursty, high-throughput streams. A small steady cluster gains little.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
question: Your app crops the 'Amount due' line from a scanned bill and calls Tesseract with default settings. It often returns an empty string even though the crop is sharp. What is the most likely first fix?
options: Retrain the LSTM model on bills
Switch to the legacy engine with --oem 0
Set the page segmentation mode to treat the image as a single line (--psm 7)
Downscale the crop so the text is smaller
explain: The default mode 3 runs full page segmentation, which expects a page of text. For a single cropped line, mode 7 tells Tesseract to skip layout analysis and read one line. Retraining or switching engines does not address the segmentation mismatch, and shrinking the text works against the 300 dpi guidance.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
question: Why does ANLS include the threshold tau instead of always scoring 1 - NL?
options: To make the metric faster to compute
So that an answer that is mostly wrong text earns nothing instead of partial credit
To handle multiple ground-truth answers
To ignore case differences
explain: Biten et al. argue that an answer more than half wrong is likely the wrong text chosen from the image, not a misread of the right text. Without the cut, random strings of the right length would collect partial credit.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
question: Your fatbin contains only an sm_86 cubin. On which GPU does the kernel load directly, with no JIT?
options: CC 8.0, since 8.0 is the base of the 8.x family
CC 9.0, since newer GPUs run older code
CC 8.9, since it has the same major and a higher minor
None, since sm_86 code always needs JIT
explain: A cubin loads on GPUs with the same major CC and a minor version greater than or equal to its own, so 8.6 and 8.9 qualify. 8.0 has a lower minor; 9.0 is a different major, and without PTX nothing can be JIT compiled.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
question: A project has 400 tests, each flaking independently at 0.5 percent per run. About what fraction of bug-free CI runs are fully green?
options: About 13 percent
About 98 percent
About 50 percent
About 0.5 percent
explain: $(1-0.005)^{400} = 0.995^{400} \approx e^{-2} \approx 0.135$. The expected number of flaky failures per run is $400 \times 0.005 = 2$, so most runs have at least one.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Giving review: reading order and comments that land
question: You are reviewing a 600-line PR. In the main file you find the data model is wrong, which will force most other files to change. You have only 20 minutes now. What should you do?
options: Finish leaving line comments on every other file first so the review is complete
Approve with a note that the design should be revisited later
Wait until you have time to review all 600 lines in one sitting
Send the design comment immediately, saying you will review the rest once the design is settled
explain: Google's guide says to send major design comments right away: much of the remaining code will change anyway, and the author may already be building on this design. Line comments on code that will be rewritten waste both people's time. Approving a known-wrong design worsens code health.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work
question: Your PR targets the `release-2.x` branch and its description says `Fixes #88`. It is merged. What happens to issue #88?
options: It closes, because Fixes is a closing keyword
It stays open, because keywords only act on PRs into the default branch
It closes only if you also wrote Fixes in the commit message
It is reopened automatically when the next release ships
explain: GitHub interprets closing keywords only when the PR targets the default branch. Otherwise no link is created and merging has no effect on the issue.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
question: You rebase a 3-commit branch onto a newer `upstream/main`. No conflicts occur, and the diffs are byte-for-byte the same. How many of your 3 commits keep their original hashes?
options: All 3, because the content did not change
Only the first, because it is closest to the base
None, because each commit's parent changed
It depends on whether you used --autosquash
explain: A commit's hash covers its tree, its parent hash, its author, committer and message. Replaying onto a new base gives the first commit a new parent, which gives it a new hash, which then changes the parent of the second commit, and so on up the chain.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
question: You modify two files of an Apache-2.0 library and ship it inside a closed-source desktop app. Which of these does Apache-2.0 require?
options: Publish the source of your app, since it contains Apache code
Nothing, because Apache-2.0 has no conditions on binaries
Include the license, mark the two files as changed, keep the existing notices and the NOTICE attributions
Get written permission from the Apache Software Foundation
explain: Section 4 lists exactly these conditions. Apache-2.0 is permissive: section 4 lets you put the larger work under your own terms, and nothing requires releasing source. The conditions do apply to binaries too: recipients must get a copy of the license.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
question: A DCO-checked PR has three commits. Which one fails?
options: Author ada@example.org, trailer Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>
A merge commit from the main branch with no trailer
Author ada@example.org, trailer Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@work.example>
Author ada@example.org with two trailers, one of them ada@example.org
explain: The DCO app requires a sign-off whose email matches the commit author. A mismatched address fails even though a sign-off exists. The app skips merge commits by default, and an extra trailer does not hurt if one matches.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
question: You want to change the documented summary of the GET command, which appears in src/commands.def. Which file should your patch edit?
options: src/commands.def, since that is where the text appears
src/commands/get.json, the input the generator reads
deps/README.md, which lists the components
src/server.c, since main() loads the command table
explain: commands.def starts with "Automatically generated ... do not edit", and the Makefile rule shows it is built from commands/*.json by utils/generate-command-code.py. Edit the JSON spec (and regenerate), otherwise the change is lost on the next build.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Find the commit behind a change: log -S, -G and -L
question: A commit changed `timeout = 30` to `timeout = 60` on the same line. Which search lists that commit?
options: `git log -S timeout`
`git log -G'timeout = '`
Both
Neither
explain: The count of "timeout" did not change (one line removed, one added), so -S skips the commit. -G matches the removed and the added line, so it lists it. `git log -S'timeout = 60'` would also work because that exact text went from 0 to 1 occurrence.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
question: A bug fails about 1 run in 20 ($p = 0.05$). You run your candidate fix 10 times and see no failures. How much does this tell you?
options: The fix works: 10 clean runs is strong evidence
Little: even without a fix, 10 runs would show no failure about 60 percent of the time
Nothing at all, because flaky bugs can never be verified
explain: With p = 0.05, the chance of zero failures in 10 runs is $0.95^{10} \approx 0.60$. You would need about 59 clean runs to rule out the original rate with 95 percent confidence, or better, find the hidden variable and make the bug deterministic.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
question: During self-review you find that your editor reformatted 300 lines in a file you only touched for a 4-line fix. What should you do?
options: Leave it; formatting changes are harmless
Mention it in the description so reviewers can skip it
Unstage the reformatting (for example with git add -p) so the PR contains only the fix; send formatting separately if the project wants it
Squash it into the fix commit so the history is shorter
explain: Accidental changes are exactly what self-review is for. They bury the real change and cause merge conflicts for others. Formatting-only changes, if wanted, are their own logical change.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
question: You run a multi-tenant API on vLLM and worry that a user could tell whether a competitor recently sent a given prompt. What does vLLM provide for this?
options: Disable PagedAttention
Set the block size to 1
Switch the hash to xxhash
A per-request cache salt mixed into the first block's hash, so only requests with the same salt share cache
explain: A shared cache leaks information through time to first token. With `cache_salt`, blocks are only shared within a trust group. A faster non-cryptographic hash like xxhash raises collision risk, which the docs warn can leak data in multi-tenant setups.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
question: Profiling a C service you built with -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Some flame graph boxes show `process` directly calling `convolve` although the code goes through `blur`. Which extra flag addresses this?
options: -fomit-frame-pointer
-mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer
-fno-inline
explain: Skipping exactly one caller is the leaf pattern: the leaf (convolve) did not set up a frame, so rbp still pointed at blur's frame and the walk jumped straight to blur's caller. Keeping frame pointers in leaf functions fixes it. Inlining blur into process could also hide it, but then the code would no longer go through a real blur frame.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Publishing an update with one 8-byte store
question: You update a 48-byte record that readers find through a pointer. Which sequence is crash-consistent without a log?
options: Overwrite the record in place, then persist it with one pmem_persist call
Write a new copy elsewhere, persist it, store the 8-byte pointer to it, persist the pointer, and free the old copy safely afterwards
Store the new pointer first so readers move quickly, then write and persist the new copy
Overwrite in place using six 8-byte stores, each one followed by CLWB but with no fences
explain: Only the out-of-place copy keeps every crash state old or new. In-place overwrite can tear across 48 bytes. Publishing the pointer first can make it durable before the data. The free must also be crash-safe, or you get a leak or a double free.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
question: The kernel docs use `struct foo { u16 field1; u32 field2; u8 field3; };`. What are its size before and after reordering to `u32, u16, u8`?
options: 12 then 8
7 then 7
8 then 8
12 then 7
explain: Original: field1 at 0, 2 pad, field2 at 4, field3 at 8, end at 9, rounded to a multiple of 4 gives 12. Reordered: 0, 4, 6, end at 7, rounded to 8. The 1 trailing byte remains, which is why it is not 7.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
question: A team swaps a 64x48 heatmap head for a 16x12 one to save compute, keeping the same decoder. What do you expect on COCO AP?
options: No change, because the quarter offset fixes quantization
An increase, because coarser maps are smoother
A drop, mostly at strict thresholds, because each cell now covers 16x16 input pixels
A drop only for keypoints that are occluded
explain: Quantization error grows with cell size, and a quarter-cell shift only removes part of it. Strict OKS thresholds such as 0.75 punish a few pixels of error, so they suffer first.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
question: With s = 0.2 and k = 10, roughly how many candidates must leave the ANN search so that at least 10 survive 99% of the time (independent filter)?
options: 50, because k / s = 50
10, because the filter cannot remove the nearest results
About 89
About 500
explain: k / s = 50 only makes the *mean* equal 10, which gives about 56% success. The binomial calculation gives K = 89 for 99%.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
question: Drepper's random list walk cost more cycles per node (450+) than the machine's raw memory latency (200 to 300). Which explanation matches Drepper's measurements?
options: The random walk executes more instructions per node
Every node also needs an address translation (TLB miss), and the hardware prefetcher wastes effort on useless lines
Random addresses bypass the cache entirely
The CPU runs at a lower clock speed during random access
explain: The loop body is identical in both layouts. Drepper attributes the extra cost to TLB misses, which add translation time to each access, and to automatic prefetching that works to a disadvantage when the pattern is random.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
question: A function zeroes a 256 MB buffer that will be filled with new data by a different stage minutes later. The machine has a 32 MB last-level cache. What does switching from ordinary stores to full-line non-temporal stores mainly save?
options: The read for ownership of every destination line, and the eviction of useful cached data
Nothing, because stores never read memory
The final sfence
Address translation for each page
explain: Ordinary stores read each line before overwriting it (RFO), so zeroing moves about twice the bytes. Full-line streaming stores skip that read and avoid flushing the cache with 256 MB of data nobody needs soon. This matches Intel's guidance for fills larger than half the LLC.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
question: A team reports their new PRM raised best-of-64 accuracy on GSM8K by 0.3 points over an ORM. What is the strongest reason to doubt that it locates errors well?
options: Best-of-N only checks final answers, so a PRM that scores like an outcome model can do well without finding step errors
0.3 points is always within noise for GSM8K
GSM8K problems have no intermediate steps
PRMs cannot be compared with ORMs
explain: The Qwen team showed best-of-N misaligns with process verification: many correct-answer responses contain flawed steps, and existing PRMs often concentrate their minimum score on the final step. A step-level benchmark such as ProcessBench tests error location directly.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
question: You benchmark a context switch with a ping-pong of two processes that touch no memory, and get 2 microseconds. Your real service switches 5,000 times a second between processes with 400 KB working sets on a CPU with a 512 KB cache. What should you expect?
options: About 1 percent overhead, since 5,000 x 2 us = 10 ms per second
No overhead, since the working sets fit in cache
Noticeably more than 1 percent, because each switch also refills cache the other process evicted, and the benchmark measured none of that
Less than 1 percent, because larger working sets amortize the switch
explain: Two 400 KB working sets do not fit in a 512 KB cache together, the regime where Li et al. saw tens to hundreds of microseconds per switch. The empty ping-pong measures only the direct cost.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
question: Your ADC distances are consistently smaller than the true distances. Is that a bug?
options: Yes: ADC should be unbiased because the query is exact
Yes: you forgot the square roots
No: the paper shows the estimator underestimates on average, and ranking does not need the bias removed
No: but you must add the correction term or recall collapses
explain: Jegou et al. show d(x, q(y)) underestimates on average. Adding the expected distortion removes the bias but increases variance, and in their experiments the corrected version gave inferior search results. Correct it only if you need the distance values themselves, for example for a radius threshold.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: A residue is a rigid frame: rotation plus translation
question: Gram-Schmidt subtracts the e1 component from the CA to N vector before normalising. What would go wrong if you skipped the subtraction and just normalised both bond vectors?
options: The matrix would still be a rotation, since both vectors have unit length
The determinant would be negative instead of positive
The third axis would be undefined because the cross product of unit vectors is zero
The two columns would not be orthogonal (the bond angle is 111.3 degrees, not 90), so R would not be in SO(3) and would distort distances
explain: Unit length is not enough: a rotation matrix needs orthogonal columns. The N-CA-C angle is about 111 degrees, so the two normalised bond vectors are not perpendicular, and a matrix built from them would stretch and shear instead of rotate.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
question: You add the rule `car, auto, automobile, vehicle` to a product search. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Precision rises and recall falls, because more terms make the query stricter
Recall rises; precision may fall because auto also appears in contexts like auto save or auto insurance
Nothing changes for ranking, because BM25 ignores terms the user did not type
Both rise with certainty, because all four words mean the same thing
explain: Expansion is an OR: more terms means more matching documents, so recall can only stay the same or rise. Whether precision suffers depends on how often the synonyms appear in other senses, as d6 and d9 show.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Why the query the user typed is rarely the query to send
question: A user searches `flew form Heathrow`. Your spelling corrector checks each word against a dictionary. What happens?
options: It rewrites form to from, because form is 2 edits from from
Nothing changes, because every word is a correctly spelled dictionary word
It rewrites Heathrow, because proper nouns are not in the dictionary
It asks did you mean, because the query returns zero results
explain: An isolated-term corrector only fires on words that are not in the dictionary. form is a real word, so it is left alone. Catching it needs context-sensitive correction, which scores combinations such as flew from by how often they occur together.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
question: A support bot gets `Which plan did I upgrade to after the billing change last March?` and the knowledge base has a general article on plan history. Which pattern fits best?
options: Step-Back: also retrieve for a broader question such as the account's plan change history
Multi-query with 3 paraphrases of the same narrow question
Spelling correction
Least-to-most on SCAN
explain: The question is narrow and time-specific, while the evidence lives in a general history document. Step-Back adds a broad query that retrieves it, and the reader picks the March change from it. Paraphrases of the narrow question share its narrowness.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
question: After rotation, the inner product between a data vector and its quantized vector is about 0.8 in high dimensions. What does this number mean?
options: The code is wrong in 20% of the bits
The estimator is accurate to within 0.2
The quantized vector is a unit vector at roughly 37 degrees from the data vector, so using it directly would shrink inner products
Only 80% of vectors get a valid code
explain: Both are unit vectors and their cosine is about 0.8 (about 37 degrees). Lesson 4 shows why treating o-bar as if it were o is biased, and how dividing by this stored 0.8-ish value fixes it.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
question: You run a 3-server cluster and add a fourth server for extra safety. How many simultaneous server failures can the cluster now survive while staying available?
options: 1, the same as before
2, one more than before
3, since one server is enough to serve reads
0, because 4 cannot form a majority
explain: With n = 4 the majority is 3, so only 1 server may be down. You added replication cost (one more copy on every write) without improving availability. Go to 5 servers to tolerate 2 failures.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
question: A team switches to lease-based reads to cut read latency. Under which condition can a client now see stale data?
options: When a follower's disk is slow
When the old leader's clock runs slow, so it keeps serving reads after a new leader has been elected
When two clients read the same key at once
Never; leases are as safe as ReadIndex
explain: A lease assumes the leader's sense of elapsed time matches the followers'. If its clock is slow or the process pauses, it may believe the lease is still valid after followers have timed out and elected someone else, and serve stale data. ReadIndex avoids this by checking with a majority on every batch of reads.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
question: A statement cites [2][5]. Passage [5] alone entails it; [2] alone does not, and [5] without [2] still entails it. How does ALCE score this?
options: Citation recall 1; citation [2] counts as irrelevant, lowering precision
Citation recall 0, because [2] does not support the statement
Citation recall 1 and precision 1, since the statement is supported
Citation recall 0.5, one supporting passage out of two
explain: Recall asks whether the concatenation of cited passages entails the statement: yes, thanks to [5]. Precision checks each citation: [2] neither supports alone nor is needed with the others, so it is irrelevant.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
question: Why do LETOR and MSLR compute BM25 separately on body, anchor, title and URL instead of once on the whole page?
options: A match in the title and a match in the body are different evidence, and separate features let the model learn a weight for each
BM25 cannot be computed on long documents
It makes the index smaller
Search engines are required to by the TREC rules
explain: Per-field (per-stream) scores keep the evidence separate. A model can then learn that a title match is worth more than a body match for this collection, which a single whole-document score cannot express.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
question: A team logs only document ids and query strings, then recomputes all features nightly for training. Which feature is most at risk of skew?
options: URL length
Number of query terms
Freshness computed from age relative to now
Whether the title contains a query term
explain: URL length, query term count and title containment are stable for a fixed document and query. Freshness relative to now is recomputed hours or days later, so every training example looks older than it was when the user saw it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
question: For a first-stage retriever whose top 100 candidates are passed to a cross-encoder reranker, which metric best measures the retriever?
options: RR, since users only look at the first result
nDCG@10 with exponential gain
R@100, the share of relevant documents that make it into the candidate set
explain: The reranker can only reorder what the retriever passes on, so the retriever's job is coverage at depth 100. Order inside the 100 matters little because the reranker rescores them. Top-heavy metrics such as RR, P@1 or nDCG@10 belong to the final ranking.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
question: A program posts receive buffers and sends but never calls `ibv_poll_cq` on a busy CQ. What happens according to the verbs documentation?
options: Old CQEs are silently overwritten and traffic continues
The NIC stops sending until the CQ has room, like TCP flow control
The kernel enlarges the CQ automatically
The CQ overruns: IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR is raised and the CQ can no longer be used
explain: The ibv_poll_cq man page warns that you must consume completions fast enough to avoid overrun; an overrun triggers IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR and the CQ becomes unusable, and the manual adds that its QPs get a fatal event. Size the CQ for the maximum number of outstanding signaled WRs and receives.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
question: Why does RoCEv2 put a UDP header in front of the IB transport header?
options: UDP provides retransmission for RDMA
UDP is required for PFC to work
To make RoCEv2 compatible with iWARP
So routers and switches can hash flows across equal-cost paths (ECMP); IP provides routing
explain: The DCQCN paper: the IP header is needed for routing, while the UDP header is needed for ECMP. Reliability still comes from the IB transport in the NIC, not from UDP.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
question: A client sends "my position is (20, 10)" every frame and the server copies it into the world. What is the core problem?
options: It uses too much bandwidth
The server cannot interpolate it
WebSocket frames cannot carry positions
The client is authoritative over its own position, so a modified client can teleport or move through walls
explain: Trusting client-reported state defeats the authoritative design. The client should send intents (move right) and the server should compute the resulting position and reject impossible moves.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
